This legal vacuum not only deepens human suffering but also creates social pressures, economic strain and, in some cases, internal security challenges for host states. The geopolitical implications of such displacement are already visible across South Asia, the Pacific and parts of coastal Africa. Despite growing awareness, the international response remains inadequate. While the United Nations, the World Bank and various regional and multilateral institutions have introduced policy frameworks and financial mechanisms to address climate change, there is still no binding international legal regime capable of confronting the existential crisis faced by island states. Debates over historical responsibility and compensation continue to divide global diplomacy. Developed industrialised countries, whose past emissions have largely driven the crisis, remain reluctant to accept legal liability, often pushing negotiations into stalemate. In response, some island states are exploring unconventional diplomatic strategies. Proposals such as digital sovereignty, purchasing land abroad, or even operating as a ‘state-in-exile’ challenge traditional notions of statehood and territoriality. While these ideas may appear radical, they reflect the depth of the crisis confronting nations whose survival is no longer guaranteed by geography alone. The broader geopolitical implications of sea level rise are difficult to ignore. Control over maritime resources, the security of sea lanes, the positioning of military infrastructure and the justification for humanitarian intervention are all increasingly shaped by climate change. Alongside conventional concepts of war and diplomacy, a new strategic reality, often described as ‘climate security’, is taking form in global politics. Sea level rise, therefore, is not merely an environmental disaster for island states. It strikes at the heart of their sovereignty, security architecture and international standing. Climate-induced displacement and disputes over maritime boundaries are set to become unavoidable features of future geopolitics. In this context, the responsibility of the international community must extend beyond expressions of sympathy. It requires the creation of binding legal frameworks, credible diplomatic initiatives and accountable global cooperation, so that vulnerable island states do not vanish from the map of history, but continue to exist as recognised and dignified members of the international community. Dr Jahangir Alam Sarker is an advocate and researcher.

title: Support to self-reliance
body: FOR millions of families in Bangladesh, poverty is not an abstract statistic. It is the daily reality of worrying about whether there will be enough food to eat, school fees to pay, or money for medicines. Nearly one in five Bangladeshis still lives below the national poverty line, with rural poverty exceeding urban rates and the risk of falling back into deprivation increasing amid economic slowdown. Within these households, women bear a disproportionate burden. Female labour force participation remains significantly lower than men’s, at roughly 42–43 per cent, and women face higher unemployment rates and greater vulnerability in informal work. Moreover, female-headed households are disproportionately concentrated among the poorest segments of society, with nearly 19 per cent located in the lowest wealth quintile. Yet for decades, most social protection programmes in Bangladesh have treated women primarily as passive recipients of aid rather than as economic actors and agents of change. This is precisely the gap that the ‘family card’ seeks to close. Under the leadership of Tarique Rahman, the Bangladesh Nationalist Party has articulated a clear and coherent vision: poverty reduction must begin with the direct empowerment of women. The proposed electronic family card has been developed within the framework of BNP’s 31-point state repair agenda, unveiled by Tarique Rahman in 2023 as a road map to rebuild institutions, restore trust and protect citizens’ basic economic security. Conceived as a transformative social protection instrument, the family card places resources, dignity and decision-making power in the hands of adult women — particularly those from poor and vulnerable households — recognising them not as dependants but as central agents of household resilience and national recovery. The family card will provide monthly food assistance equivalent to Tk 2,000–2,500 per family, delivered either through direct cash transfers or in-kind food support. The essential food basket under consideration includes staples such as 20–25 kilograms of rice, 2–3 kilograms of wheat flour, 2 kilograms of lentils (dal), and 1–1.5 litres of cooking oil per month. These items form the basic nutritional backbone of a typical Bangladeshi household. To ensure effectiveness, transparency and public confidence, the BNP plans to pilot the programme in one upazila from each division, carefully assessing operational feasibility, beneficiary preferences and delivery mechanisms. Based on evidence from these rapidly conducted pilots, the most efficient and preferred option will be scaled up, initially covering 50 lakh families, with a clear and credible pathway towards nationwide roll-out. A defining feature of the family card is its blanket, non-targeted approach. Instead of selective beneficiary lists — which are often vulnerable to corruption, favouritism and exclusion — the programme will distribute family cards universally at the household level. As Tarique Rahman has repeatedly emphasised in his public speeches, ‘When assistance depends on selection, corruption enters through the back door. When rights are universal, dignity is protected.’ This design minimises administrative discretion, sharply reduces leakages, and helps restore public trust in social protection delivery. When everyone is eligible, no one needs political connections to survive. Crucially, the family card will be issued in the name of the adult female head of the household. This is not symbolic; it is strategic. By reducing monthly food expenditure by around Tk 2,000, women will be able to accumulate savings over time. These savings can be invested in small income-generating activities — home-based enterprises, poultry rearing, tailoring, food processing or petty trade — transforming subsistence households into self-reliant ones. In this sense, the family card is not merely a safety net; it is a springboard for women’s economic empowerment. Bangladesh has witnessed the power of such ideas before. In 1992–93, the then prime minister Khaleda Zia introduced the internationally acclaimed ‘food for education’ (and later ‘cash for education’) programme. By linking food support to schooling, that initiative helped pull millions of children — especially girls — out of illiteracy and into classrooms, laying the foundation for long-term human development. The family card builds directly on that legacy but adapts it to today’s realities. If Food for Education empowered young girls through learning, the family card is designed to empower adult women through economic security, savings, and pathways to self-reliance — transforming support into opportunity and dependence into dignity. Globally, evidence strongly supports this approach. Studies by the World Bank and United Nations agencies consistently show that transfers directed to women improve household nutrition, children’s education, and long-term productivity. Women are more likely to invest resources in family welfare and income-generating activities. By channelling support directly to women, the family card aligns Bangladesh’s social protection system with proven international best practice. Most importantly, the family card reflects a deeper political philosophy. It recognises women not as dependants, but as partners in national development. It acknowledges unpaid care work, informal labour and women’s central role in household resilience. It also sends a powerful message: poverty reduction is not charity — it is an investment in human potential. At a time when economic pressures are intensifying and inequality threatens social cohesion, the family card offers a bold yet practical solution. It is fiscally manageable, administratively transparent and socially transformative. Above all, it restores dignity to women who have long carried the burden of poverty without recognition or support. By advancing the family card, Tarique Rahman and the BNP are proposing more than a welfare programme. They are proposing a new social contract — one in which empowering women becomes the foundation of a fairer, more resilient Bangladesh. Dr Ziauddin Hyder is an adviser to the chairperson of the Bangladesh Nationalist Party and former World Bank senior health and nutrition specialist.

title: Cinema as witness to time
body: CINEMA began not as a fiction, but as a document. The history of cinema is celebrated around the globe every year on December 28 and one might argue that it is done so wrongfully. When we speak of World Cinema Day, we often narrate it as the day when the first cinema was created. Similarly, when speaking of the Lumière brothers, they are often described as the inventors of cinema. While this stems from a famous misconception, the real question is why public consciousness prioritises the 1895 screenings over earlier milestones in the history of cinema, such as Louis le Prince’s Roundhay Garden Scene, filmed in October 1888. Le Prince’s filmmaking process inspired thousands, including the likes of Thomas Edison and Georges Melies. Edison began creating motion pictures that recorded lived realities; athletic displays, Native American traditions, rituals, different forms of dance, even scandalous dance performances became the subject of his cinema. Films such as Dickson Greeting, Newark Athlete, and Men Boxing (1891) were among the first moving images ever recorded on celluloid. This also goes to show that cinema, from its inception, was entangled with spectacle, labour, gender, and, most importantly, the political landscape of a society. But the most interesting fact is the term used for such films. Early film historians use the term ‘actuality’ to describe these short non-fiction films produced during the first decade of motion picture history. In modern discourse, the term itself holds connotations that extend far beyond the technical definitions assigned by early historians. We now understand recording itself as a political act. Society dictates who, what and how things are to be recorded. And so the term ‘actuality’ serves as a fitting designation for cinema, since it possesses the unique capacity to capture the moral and social truths of its time. Initially, individuals would peer through the hole of a Kinetoscope to view realities that were already visible to them. Perhaps that experience was able to offer a perspective that the unmediated reality could not. Either way, as Edison’s Kinetoscope gained popularity, the demand for new subjects expanded. War and disaster soon became central subjects. Through these films, cinema functioned as an early visual archive of modern history. Yet despite this vast documentary impulse, Edison’s cinema remained largely private. In theory, there is nothing inherently wrong with cinema being viewed individually. Many modern filmmakers deliberately resist open commercial circulation and prefer to screen their films in closed, controlled, or semi-private contexts. Even then, the experience is often shared among like-minded peers. However, the Kinetoscope was restricted to a single viewer at a time. This changed decisively with the invention of the Cinematographe, which, for the first time, enabled cinema to be screened for a public audience. The Lumière brothers, Auguste and Louis, arranged the first public screening of a movie in Paris in 1895, featuring films like Workers Leaving the Lumière Factory. This event transformed the possibilities cinema had to offer by creating a collective viewing experience. While the Kinetoscope functioned as a voyeuristic device, the Cinematographe became a democratic one. Cinema moved from the peephole to the screen, from individual curiosity to shared spectatorship. Even the word ‘cinema’ was not originally intended to describe the flickering light alone; it was the name of the space where movies are to be screened. To name the art after the space it occupies is to admit that its very soul is social, that it exists not in the isolation of the eye, but in the collective breathing of the crowd. Thus, early cinema was defined by two foundational qualities: the ability to document reality and the power to reach the masses. While Le Prince and many others can be accredited as the first filmmakers, history chooses to remember the Lumière brothers for establishing cinema as a public, social event on December 28, 1895. On World Cinema Day, we remember the social nature of cinema to understand the power the screen holds to remember, narrate, and deliver. It is a vessel designed to hold what the world tries to discard; memories of injustice, the cold weight of violence, and the silent machinery of exploitation. And it does more than just narrate loss and grief. It carries our everyday dreams and stubborn hopes, and that persistent ache for a better world, delivering them from the individual consciousness to the public eye. In times like these, the philosophical argument regarding the ethics of a filmmaker or a film activist is no longer a theoretical debate, but a social reality, a burden of truth that the artist must carry. Ania Fahmin is a student of anthropology at the University of Dhaka.

title: Issues for govt to fix to deal with surplus agricultural output
body: A RECORD record potato harvest this season for farmers in the north has become a stark illustration of how abundance can paradoxically breed disaster. What should have been a period of relative prosperity has instead turned into a likely financial crisis as prices have plummeted to levels far below production costs. Early potatoes, expected to bring a premium before the main harvest, are now sold for Tk 10–12 a kilogram, barely a half of what it cost to produce them. The situation is compounded by the lingering stock of the past season’s crop in cold storage, creating an unprecedented ‘double blow’ for growers who hoped for stable returns. Government efforts to safeguard the sector, including a minimum price announcement and plans for procurement, have largely remained unimplemented, leaving farmers to navigate the collapse unaided. Rising input costs, from fertiliser and fuel to labour, have exacerbated the imbalance between cost and revenue while weak market forecasting and ineffective regulation have allowed surplus supply to overwhelm demand. Beyond the immediate losses, the crisis exposes structural vulnerabilities in agricultural markets. The crisis at hand underscores the urgent need for a cold storage system that is both accessible and efficiently managed. While the government has established 384 commercial cold storage units with a combined capacity of around 3.27 million tonnes and more than 650 low-cost attic-style facilities in village, the measures fall far short of the nation’s annual potato output of 11.5 million tonnes. Even where space exists, high storage rents, sometimes exceeding the market value of the potatoes, leave many farmers reluctant to store their crops while poorly maintained units risk spoilage. Expanding storage capacity, reducing costs and ensuring proper upkeep are essential first steps, but they should also be paired with investment in agricultural processing industry and value addition. Limited processing facilities, weak export channels and the absence of a coordinated cold-chain logistics network prevent surplus potatoes from reaching alternative markets. Without reforms to market regulation, price stabilisation mechanisms and a strategic push into processing and export infrastructure, any expansion in storage will merely postpone the inevitable price collapse. A comprehensive approach is needed, one that combines storage improvements, market management and processing initiatives to protect farmers and stabilise the sector against both seasonal and structural vulnerabilities. The authorities should act decisively to prevent repeated losses. Expanding and properly managing cold storage, investing in processing and export infrastructure and enforcing market regulation are essential. Without these measures, farmers will continue to bear the brunt of surplus and price collapse, rural livelihood will be jeopardised and seasonal gluts will remain a persistent threat to both food security and agricultural stability.

title: Jamaat’s ruse of religion calls for early EC, govt action
body: THE Bangladesh Jamaat-e-Islami’s ruse of religious sentiments to curry votes in the run-up to the national elections set for February 12, as New Age reported on December 27, is troublesome. Party leaders, mainly at the grass roots, have started using religious sentiments of the Muslims in their electoral campaigns, claiming that it is the religious responsibility of the people to cast their vote for Jamaat-e-Islami and a deviation from this would harm their faith. With such campaigns that exploit the faith of the Muslims having begun, the video clips of which have already gone viral on social media platforms, political analysts, rights activists and civil society actors are worried as such a practice could undermine democratic norms and fuel a social polarisation. They are rightly worried as such campaigns heavily laced with religious sentiments would destabilise the electoral environment by not only creating a fearful situation and embracing an approach to coercion but also adding to sectarian tension. All this continues to happen in contravention of the electoral code of conduct, Political Parties and Candidates’ Code of Conduct 2025, which the Election Commission officially notified on November 10 in view of the national elections. Rule 16 (a) of the electoral code of conduct lays out a bar on the abuse of religious or racial sentiments for electoral gains while Rule 15 (b) places a bar on the use of places of worship, public offices and educational institutions for electoral campaigns. Allegations are rife that Jamaat leaders and activists are asking people to vote for Jamaat candidates in the elections to ensure their ‘berth for heaven (Jannah)’ and a failure to do so would harm their faith. One of Jamaat’s aspirant candidates for a Kushtia constituency is reported to have said that casting a vote for Jamaat would earn voters the reward equivalent to the prayers of 180 million people. Thoughtful sections of society believe that such an exploitation of people’s faith by Jamaat-e-Islami through deceitful means is unethical and borders on sacrilege. They say that Jamaat’s switch between religion and coercion, whichever suits its interests best, also breaks the established political norms and jeopardises the tenet that the country is home to multiple religions where people of every faith enjoy full religious freedom. They further say that Jamaat-e-Islami deliberately plays with people’s faith and religious sentiments to consolidate its voter base and to deflect the criticism of the party’s political agenda and historical records. One of Jamaat’s assistant secretaries general seeks to say that the party does not allow the use of religion in electoral campaigns, but reported instances of the abuse of religious sentiment negates the party’s stated position. The situation, therefore, warrants an early, decisive action of both the Election Commission and the government on Jamaat’s ruse of religion in electoral campaigns.

title: Ending wars and restarting factories
body: While industrialisation remains a top priority for Global South countries, debt-driven austerity, corporate dominance, wars and sanctions keep many poorer nations locked into dependency and underdevelopment, writes Vijay Prashad IN MID-NOVEMBER 2025, at a United Nations Industrial Development Organisation conference in Saudi Arabia, Basher Abdullah, an adviser to Sudan’s ministry of industry and trade, said, ‘First, we need to end the war. Then, we have to restart the factories.’ His comment was about Sudan’s appalling civil war, but it could have been about many countries in the global south that are in the midst of either a shooting war or a trade war. For these poorer nations, development has been set aside in favour of more immediate threats. Yet beyond the horizon of guns and extortion lies the need to imagine possible futures. The UNIDO conference acknowledged that industrialisation is ‘essential for achieving the [UNs] Sustainable Development Goals’ and that to do so ‘a new industrial deal’ is needed. A UNIDO policy brief from April 2025 identifies many obstacles to industrialisation in the global south, including deficits in infrastructure, limited technological and scientific capacity, a lack of highly trained workers, and weak logistical networks, including digital infrastructure. The brief also notes ‘megatrends’ that the global south needs to follow and adapt to, such as digitalisation and the rise of artificial intelligence, the reconfiguration of global value chains, the energy transition, and demographic changes. These trends, the brief argues, represent risks as well as opportunities. But where will the poorer nations get the investment for infrastructure, new skills and cleaner industries? How will they be able to leapfrog older, more polluting industrial models and integrate into modern production chains? Conferences like the one in Saudi Arabia rarely reflect on the constraints faced by the poorer nations and the structural deindustrialisation they have experienced. Deindustrialisation in the global south is neither accidental nor the product of ‘internal inefficiencies,’ as International Monetary Fund economists argue. It is a direct result of the third world debt crisis that erupted in the early 1980s and the structural adjustment programmes enforced by the IMF and the World Bank over the 1980s and 1990s. In the 1980s, for instance, IMF policies forced tariff reductions that exposed Ghana’s textile and garment factories to cheap imports, causing Accra’s once-thriving industrial belt to collapse. In Zambia in the 1990s, SAPs led to the privatisation of industries supplying copper mines, dismantling local fabrication foundries, machine shops, and chemical plants that formed the industrial base in the Copperbelt. In Brazil’s ABC industrial belt south of São Paulo and in the manufacturing corridors of Greater Buenos Aires, debt-era austerity, currency devaluations, and rapid trade liberalisation in the 1980s and 1990s pushed automobile, metalworking and textile plants to shed jobs, close, or relocate as markets were opened to cheaper imports. Across the Global South, peripheral economies that had begun to industrialise were pushed back into a familiar pattern of exporting raw materials and importing manufactures — the very structure of the neocolonial economy. There is also scant attention paid to the violence — of wars and sanctions — that destabilise sovereign states and derail the industrial aspirations of the poorer nations. Conflict destroys industrial infrastructure and fragments and demoralises the working class, both of which are essential to development. Only a few countries in the global south have been able to defend against these assaults on their sovereignty and nurture their industrial capacity. The most remarkable example is Cuba, which has been able to develop its industrial capacity in biotechnology, medical equipment and pharmaceuticals despite a brutal six-decade blockade — a case of socialist industrialisation under siege. Vietnam is another example: despite being devastated by imperialist wars, it was nonetheless able to recover thanks to state-directed industrial policy that built manufacturing capacity in textiles, electronics and shipbuilding. The most successful example, of course, is China, which used state planning, decentralised governance and public ownership of the commanding heights of the economy — including finance and technology — to build an industrial powerhouse and lift 800 million people out of extreme poverty over the past four decades. Taken together, these experiences contradict every neoliberal developmentalist prescription given to the poorer nations of the global south. Industrial policy is not merely a technical exercise but a political one. It is about building the conditions for industrial development by asserting sovereignty and the right to development and by building working-class power through class struggle. A ‘new industrial deal’ cannot be implemented if a country is systematically derailed by IMF-driven austerity, multinational corporations that dominate raw-material extraction and exports and the violence of wars and sanctions. Together, these forces destroy productive infrastructure, shrink state capacity and produce a precarious and politically weakened peasantry and working class, undermining democratic processes and making planning impossible. Unless there is sovereignty, there can be no new industrial deal. Over the past few years, Tricontinental: Institute for Social Research has been elaborating a new development theory for the global south. Within this framework, it has identified the following preconditions for industrialisation: Workers as central planners. Planning must be democratised, as in the Indian state of Kerala, which in 1996 launched the People’s Plan Campaign for Decentralised Planning. Industrialisation cannot be accomplished unless planning includes inputs from workers and peasants’ organisations and other popular bodies rooted in local communities. Restoring sovereignty. Wars must end, sanctions must be lifted and governments must be given the space to build state capacity for long-term planning, including investment in infrastructure, transport and logistics that can link producers and consumers across regions and lower the costs of development. Overcoming dependency. To overcome dependency, state policy must be able to protect domestic industries using tariffs and subsidies, regulate finance through capital controls and ensure technology and knowledge transfer. This will allow countries to move from raw-material-exporting economies to ones grounded in diversified domestic manufacturing. Expanding public ownership. Strategic sectors of the economy — such as land, finance, energy, minerals, transport and capital goods — must be publicly controlled to ensure that they operate for national development rather than private profit. Public sector firms and institutions, as Meng Jie and Zhang Zibin showed with China’s high-technology sector, can compete and create a public market that increases efficiencies. Building south-south cooperation. Countries in Africa, Asia and Latin America must increase cooperation — reviving the Bandung Spirit — in order to break the role of Western monopoly firms and structures in the areas of finance and technology. A decade ago, at the 2015 Forum on China-Africa Cooperation in Johannesburg, South Africa, the Chinese government and fifty African governments discussed the problem of economic development and industrialisation. Since 1945, the question of African industrialisation has been on the table but has not advanced due to the neocolonial structure that has prevented any serious structural transformation. The most industrialised countries on the African continent are South Africa, Morocco and Egypt, but the entire continent accounts for less than 2 percent of world manufacturing value added and only about 1 percent of global trade in manufactures. That is why it was so significant for FOCAC to put industrial policy at the heart of its agenda; its 2015 Johannesburg Declaration affirmed that ‘industrialisation is an imperative to ensure Africa’s independent and sustainable development.’ China’s industrial capacity would be put at the service of Africa’s need for industrialisation through the creation of joint ventures, industrial parks, a cooperation fund and mechanisms for technology and science transfer. Africa-China trade has increased from $10 billion in 2000 to $282 billion in 2023. In 2024, the Chinese government upgraded its relationship with African states to ‘strategic partnerships,’ enabling greater cooperation. We now have a test case for whether South-South cooperation can engender sovereign industrialisation that breaks with the old patterns of plunder and dependency. Ultimately, African governments, workers, and movements will have to wield these ties as instruments of development rather than allow them to become yet another regime of unequal exchange. At stake in all these debates about industrialisation is a simple question: will the resources of the Global South be used to enrich a few or to sustain life for the many? Reading about FOCAC reminded me of Nigerian poet Niyi Osundare (born 1947), whose book The Eye of the Earth (1986) includes powerful poems about humanity’s relationship with nature. One poem in that collection — ‘Ours to Plough Not to Plunder’ — became so iconic that it was taught to generations of Nigerian schoolchildren, despite repression under the military government that took power in 1983. Here are the last two stanzas: Our earth is an unopened grainhouse, a bustling barn in some far, uncharted jungle a distant gem in a rough unhappy dust. This earth is ours to work not to waste ours to man not to maim. This earth is ours to plough, not to plunder. Consortiumnews.com, December 23, 2025. Vijay Prashad is an Indian historian, editor and journalist. He is a writing fellow and chief correspondent at Globetrotter. He is an editor of LeftWord Books and the director of Tricontinental: Institute for Social Research.

title: Osman Hadi, Abu Sayeed and Abrar Fahad
body: DEATH is the ultimate and inescapable destiny of human life. No matter how mighty one is or how desperately one wishes to cling to life, death will embrace them. Fir’aun (Pharaoh), the ancient Egyptian ruler, arrogated to himself the godly status, but the aquatic end of his life proved that he was no more than humans. He died a humiliating death. Conversely, there are deaths that ennoble lives, making them unforgettable. These are deaths of those who risk not dying a natural death for a higher calling. Those whose lives are snatched away rather prematurely by forces of evil; those who lived more for others than for themselves; those who could have given so much more had they lived longer to reach the full potential in their lives. By taking those exceptional lives, their killers not only eliminate them but also rob society and humanity of gems and treasures. However, these are deaths which are also deathless. Paradoxically, their death promises a longer life — a life which cannot be touched by death any more and secured from oblivion. Osman Hadi, Abu Sayeed and Abrar Fahad are blessed with such deaths and deathlessness. They met the tragic end of their lives at the hand of their killers at young ages. However, their deaths have an indelible print on our minds. One other such death is that of president Ziaur Rahman. Hadi and Ziaur Rahman embraced martyrdom 44 years apart. In both cases, the city of Dhaka was turned into a funeral prayer site. Abu Sayeed and Abrar Fahad did not have such funeral congregations because Hasina’s autocracy did not allow people to congregate to show their last respect to them. Hadi, Sayeed, and Abrar all lost their lives essentially for the same cause. It is justice, dignity and freedom. It is for speaking or standing against the hegemony of a regional superpower and its local agents. Their killers, architects and financiers belonged to the same political tribe. It is surprising that those who caused their deaths claimed to be associated with our national independence in 1971. They presented themselves as the sole agent of our freedom from Pakistani colonialism. However, it is now clear that they wanted to free us from Pakistan to sell our freedom to India. Such a reading may appear one-sidedly preposterous. However, we just need to consider the current location of the Awami forces, including their leader and the havoc they have been wreaking on our country. We should also recollect who they truly served during their autocratic rule. Abrar Fahad was a promising student at the Bangladeshi University of Engineering and Technology. As a young man of dignity, freedom, and justice and a patriotic citizen, he could not accept the Awami government’s servitude to India. He spoke against bilateral treaties which were unfair and unjust to Bangladesh. In any democratic and independent nation, Abrar would have been commended for his visceral nationalistic sentiments. However, he could not expect anything better when the government in power acted as an agent of their Indian master. Abrar was beaten to death with unprecedented cruelty by those who were called the golden children of the so-called pro-independent forces. What an irony! That irony is now clear. We now know who are for and against dependence or independence of our hapless nation. Abrar was killed in the most barbaric manner, but he has not died. Chhatra League hooligans, in fact, brought him a life beyond death. This writing itself is evidence of his living and being remembered with love and respect. Abu Sayeed was the catalyst of the July 2024 movement which freed the country not only from Hasina’s autocracy but also from the hegemonic patron of her misrule. He embraced the bullets of the Awami police. His way of giving life is exceptional not only in this country but, maybe, in the whole world. Bullets took his mortal life but gave him some kind of immortality in return. Those who love Bangladesh and those who love freedom and justice will love Abu Syeed. He will never be forgotten. By embracing death, he showed us how to live. The unbearable death of Osman Hadi is still fresh with us. The soil of his grave on the central mosque premises of the University of Dhaka has not yet settled. His killers took his life because he challenged the established political elitism and, thus, became the voice of Bangladesh in the post-autocracy era. He embodied what the best Bangladeshi looks like — pious without prejudice, honest without pretension and humble without exception. He was a loving father and an admired husband. He was not a politician, but still he showed us how to do politics, lead our nation and love our country. He gave us an outstanding example of how to live, even if living meant holding life in your hands. He taught us how to speak fearlessly, no matter what price must be paid for speaking. Of the many voices that have been active in politics and media in recent Bangladesh, his was the most authentic one, commanding an audience. A voice that people from all walks of life — except those of the hegemonic forces — gave a hearing. A voice that was polite and courteous but never missed to point out the root cause of our dirty and deplorable politics. Abrar dreamt of a free Bangladesh; Sayeed wished for a Bangladesh that would be free from autocrats; Hadi wanted a Bangladesh where people would live with dignity with other nations in the region and beyond. Unfortunately, their lives were cut short before their wishes and dreams could materialise. These best and most promising of Bangladeshis were killed by the same evil forces of servitude, autocracy and moral bankruptcy. They eliminated the best sons of the soil so the country could continue serving the hegemonic interests of a regional big brother. We as a nation have a colossal debt of gratitude to them. We also have a great responsibility towards them for our own interest. First, we must do the opposite of what their killers did — they sought to erase them from Bangladesh’s map, mind and mission. We should establish them more firmly everywhere, in politics, education, culture and history. We will tell their killers that the trios are more alive after their deaths and that their voices of resistance are more commanding now than when they lived. Second, we should sustain their legacy of justice, truth and freedom. Those who intend to compromise these ideals, those who seek alliance with their killers, should be rejected not just through the ballot but also socially, politically and culturally. Third, no matter which party rules this country, the courage and heroism of these souls must be invested, utilised and immortalised so that we have their likes in the future. We need to create more Abrars, more Hadis, more Sayeeds and innumerable other July 2024 martyrs and warriors so that their legacy can continue. We need them across generations who will keep telling us that the value of life lies in giving it selflessly when needed. That true honour and dignity do not lie in slavery or in running away; that life gathers its meaning when death can be embraced without compromising higher ideals. Bangladesh cannot afford to forget these great souls. They must live in our heart, on pages of our books, in our soil and in the air. Like Laurence Binyon in his poem ‘For the Fallen’, we should recite: They shall grow not old, as we that are left grow old: Age shall not weary them, nor the years condemn. At the going down of the sun and in the morning We will remember them. Obaidul Hamid is an associate professor at the University of Queensland in Australia. He researches language, education, and society in the developing world. He is a co-editor of Current Issues in Language Planning.

title: Opinion/Editorial
body: When crowd watches man burn IN MYMENSINGH, a man named Dipu Chandra Das was beaten to death. After his life had been extinguished, his body was tied to a tree in a public square and set on fire. Around him, a crowd gathered in total silence. Not a single voice rose to stop...

title: When crowd watches man burn
body: IN MYMENSINGH, a man named Dipu Chandra Das was beaten to death. After his life had been extinguished, his body was tied to a tree in a public square and set on fire. Around him, a crowd gathered in total silence. Not a single voice rose to stop it. Not a single hand reached to intervene. Some recorded the scene on their phones; others simply stood, watching. In that silence, the crime became larger than the attackers, it became the reflection of a society that has stopped feeling, a conscience suspended, if not lost entirely. This was not a sudden, uncontrollable chaos. It unfolded in stages, in public, giving every observer the opportunity to act differently. Yet nobody did. That total passivity speaks to something far deeper than lawlessness: a moral collapse, a desensitisation so profound that witnessing atrocity is no longer shocking but banal. Psychologists describe this phenomenon as diffusion of responsibility and moral disengagement. In a crowd, individuals feel shielded by the presence of others. The mind rationalises: someone else will intervene, it is not my duty, I am merely an observer. Filming becomes a substitute for action; silence becomes complicity. Public indifference is not accidental, it is learned. Moral numbness grows where empathy is conditional, outrage is selective and violence is normalised as spectacle. When human life can be desecrated in public without anyone speaking out, something foundational has eroded — not only law, but the very fabric of humanity. The justification offered for Dipu’s killing, that he allegedly made comments about the Prophet Muhammad (PBUH), reveals another layer of distortion. Nothing about this act aligns with the ethical teachings of Islam. The Qur’an is unequivocal: ‘Whoever kills a soul unless for a soul or for corruption in the land, it is as if he has killed all of humanity.’ (Qur’an 5:32) The life of the Prophet Muhammad demonstrates moral clarity. He endured insult, mockery and physical attack, yet he never sanctioned mob violence. He emphasised restraint, mercy and due process — even toward those who harmed him. Faith, he demonstrated, is measured not by anger or retaliation, but by moral courage and compassion. If the Prophet were to witness a body being burned in the street while bystanders remained silent, he would call it zulm — oppression. Religion without humanity is hollow. Justice without law is cruelty. It is time for Bangladesh and for the wider Muslim world to re-examine Islam and question what is being taught in madrasas across the country. But the issue is not confined to madrasas. It is the broader interpretation of Islam circulating in society: one that spreads fear rather than understanding, rigidity rather than reflection, obedience rather than ethical inquiry. Globally, distorted versions of religion have stifled progress. Countries like Iran and Afghanistan were once far more open, diverse and progressive. Today, they have been pulled backward, their societies shaped by rigid ideologies that prioritise control over human flourishing. If we do not question the religion we practice and the teachings we pass to our children, we are abandoning ourselves. Religion is, at its core, a quest for understanding, a path toward discovering our own selves and our purpose in this life. When that quest leads to moral paralysis, when it allows a crowd to stand silently while a man is burned alive, it is failing its fundamental purpose. Distortions of Islam have deep roots in history. During the Cold War, simplified and militant interpretations were encouraged as tools of geopolitical strategy. Religion became a weapon — mobilised, manipulated and hardened into a version of orthodoxy that departed from centuries of ethical scholarship and moral reasoning. Over time, these ideologies created societies where fear replaces reflection, obedience replaces conscience and violence is justified in the name of faith. The consequences are clear: crowds form before facts are known, rumours spread faster than reason and technology turns human suffering into spectacle. Empathy is replaced by detachment; moral courage by passive observation. And the cycle continues. Bangladesh must confront an urgent question: what are we teaching our people to feel? Laws alone cannot repair a society’s conscience. Arrests and condemnations after the fact cannot restore empathy that has been systematically eroded. If belief systems discourage ethical reflection and reward rage, mobs will continue to form, and bystanders will continue to watch in silence. An evolved society does not abandon faith. It returns to conscience. It teaches that belief demands responsibility, that justice requires process and that no crowd has the right to determine life or death. It teaches that mercy is strength and that restraint is moral courage. It teaches that religion is not a tool for fear or control, but a guide for understanding, self-discovery and the pursuit of a life worth living. A man was beaten to death in Mymensingh and his body was burned in public while the crowd looked on, silent. The question is not what he was accused of saying. The question is: what have we become and what will we do to reclaim our humanity? Anusheh Anadil is a singer and social activist.

title: Naming torture, restoring dignity
body: TORTURE is a grave violation of human rights and human dignity, inflicting not only immediate suffering but enduring physical, psychological and social harm. In societies where arbitrary detention, political violence and coercive interrogation persist, the systematic identification and documentation of torture survivors is a necessary step towards justice, rehabilitation and prevention. Central to this process is the development of reliable screening instruments that allow healthcare professionals, legal practitioners and human rights defenders to recognise, record and respond to torture ethically and effectively. Recent international initiatives led by research institutions have strengthened the scientific and ethical foundations of such tools, underscoring the need for careful adaptation across cultural and clinical contexts. Identifying survivors of torture involves navigating a complex intersection of legal definitions, clinical manifestations and social realities. Under the United Nations Convention Against Torture, torture is defined in absolute terms as the intentional infliction of severe physical or mental suffering for specific purposes, including punishment or extraction of information. Effective identification therefore requires a clear understanding of both the definition and the varied methods of torture — such as beatings, electric shocks, positional abuse or sensory deprivation — each leaving distinct physical and psychological traces. In Bangladesh and comparable settings, investigative reports and survivor accounts point to the continued use of abusive practices in custodial environments. Survivors often describe prolonged beatings or electric shocks that result in lasting trauma, impaired mental health and fractured social relationships. Yet disclosure remains difficult. Fear of retaliation, stigma and the absence of trauma-sensitive assessment mechanisms frequently silence survivors. These barriers make the case for validated, context-sensitive screening instruments not only practical but ethically imperative. Screening tools for torture aim to ensure accurate identification while minimising the risk of harm or misclassification. One internationally recognised example is the structured instrument developed by Dignity, the Danish Institute Against Torture, in collaboration with partner organisations. This tool combines initial screening questions about arrest, detention and exposure to violence with narrative prompts that allow survivors to describe their experiences in their own words. These accounts are then assessed against criteria such as severity, intent and perpetrator identity, in line with international legal standards. Validation of such instruments requires rigorous methodological processes to ensure reliability across languages and cultures. Lessons can be drawn from the adaptation of the Harvard Trauma Questionnaire, which has been widely used among refugee populations to assess both torture exposure and trauma-related symptoms. Its validation underscores the importance of cultural adaptation, expert review and empirical testing. Similar steps — item mapping, pilot testing, survivor consultation and iterative refinement — are essential for torture screening tools, particularly in contexts like Bangladesh, where linguistic diversity and social norms shape how trauma is expressed. Ethical considerations lie at the heart of screening and documentation. The process must respect survivors’ dignity, autonomy and safety, especially where the alleged perpetrators are state actors. Principles such as informed consent, confidentiality and non-maleficence are not optional but foundational. The Istanbul Protocol, the international standard for the documentation of torture, emphasises collaboration between clinicians and legal professionals to ensure that documentation is both medically sound and legally robust. Ethical screening also requires training in trauma-informed communication. Survivors should be supported to share their experiences in a non-coercive environment, with a clear understanding of how their information will be used. Secure data management is equally vital. While aggregated data is crucial for advocacy, rehabilitation planning and policy reform, inadequate safeguards can expose survivors to further risk. Ethical oversight and secure record-keeping are therefore essential. The consequences of torture extend far beyond physical injury. Survivors frequently experience chronic pain, anxiety, depression, post-traumatic stress and social dislocation. Identification is only meaningful if it leads to comprehensive care. Rehabilitation must integrate physical treatment, mental health support and social reintegration. Organisations such as Dignity have demonstrated that trauma-informed psychosocial care, including interventions delivered by trained non-specialists, can be effective even in resource-constrained settings. In Bangladesh, where mental health services remain limited, validated screening tools can help allocate scarce resources more effectively. Early and accurate identification allows service providers to design tailored rehabilitation pathways that combine healthcare, legal assistance and community support. This approach recognises rehabilitation not as charity, but as a matter of rights and dignity. Systematic identification and documentation also carry broader legal and institutional significance. When collected ethically and in line with international standards, evidence of torture can support legal redress, compensation claims and advocacy for reform. Aggregated data from validated instruments can reveal patterns of abuse, strengthening national and international monitoring mechanisms. Civil society organisations in Bangladesh, including the Centre for Rehabilitation of Torture Survivors, already play a crucial role in identifying victims, providing care and raising awareness. The wider adoption of validated screening tools would strengthen these efforts by improving data quality and evidentiary credibility. International frameworks such as the Istanbul Protocol further ensure that documentation can withstand judicial scrutiny, whether in domestic courts or international forums. Despite its importance, implementing systematic torture screening in Bangladesh faces obstacles. Limited professional training, resource constraints and political sensitivities surrounding torture documentation remain significant challenges. Addressing them requires sustained investment in capacity-building, institutional collaboration and the integration of screening protocols into health, justice and detention-monitoring systems. International partnerships with organisations such as the International Rehabilitation Council for Torture Victims and Dignity can provide technical support and facilitate culturally appropriate adaptation. Screening, however, cannot stand alone. Without accessible rehabilitation and follow-up services, identification risks reopening wounds without offering pathways to healing. A survivor-centred approach demands that screening be matched by investment in psychosocial care, legal aid and reintegration programmes. Recognising torture survivors through validated, ethical screening is a cornerstone of any serious human rights response to torture. In Bangladesh, adapting such tools to local realities, while grounding them in international standards can strengthen rehabilitation, accountability and prevention. Naming torture is the first step towards restoring dignity. Ensuring that recognition leads to care, justice and reform is the responsibility that follows. Musharraf Tansen is a development analyst and former country representative of the Malala Fund.

title: Cold wave calls for early, coordinated response
body: THE mild cold wave sweeping over the north for the third consecutive day has disrupted daily life, especially in Rangpur division and adjoining districts along the Brahmaputra basin, exposing once again the seasonal vulnerability of the region’s poorest communities. Despite a slight increase in daytime temperatures and largely unchanged night-time lows, the intensity of the cold has remained steady, accompanied by dense fog and cold winds from the west and north-west. Minimum temperatures hovered around 10–11 degrees Celsius in Rangpur, Dinajpur and Kurigram while daytime warmth offered only brief relief when the sun broke through for a few hours in the afternoon. Economic activity slowed as many people stayed indoors and reports from hospitals indicate a fresh increae in the number of patients suffering from cold-related illnesses. The impact has been most severe in riverbank and char areas, where fragile housing and limited access to heating acutely expose people to winter conditions. In response, the district administrations and non-governmenal and voluntary organisations have begun distributing blankets and warm clothes, supported by government allocations of funds and relief materials. While authorities report adequate medical preparedness and ongoing relief efforts, life for thousands in remote and low-income communities remains significantly disrupted by the cold spell. The persistence cold spell serves as a reminder of the importance of consistent preparedness in public healthcare facilities beyond the capital, where seasonal weather events place recurring pressure on local services. Although health authorities report adequate stocks of essential medicines, reports show that district and upazila hospitals, particularly those in riverine and char areas, often face a sudden increase in patients with respiratory and cold-related illnesses once temperatures fall. Effective preparedness, therefore, requires more than supply availability. It depends on timely coordination between meteorological forecasts and health responses, adequate staffing during peak periods and outreach mechanisms for hard-to-reach communities. Relief initiatives, including the ongoing distribution of blankets and warm clothes by government agencies and partner organisations remains a necessary part of the response, yet its impact is shaped by the speed, coverage and consistency of delivery. Given that winter cold is a predictable seasonal challenge in the north, a more structured and anticipatory approach would reduce reliance on ad hoc measures. Alongside institutional efforts, there is also space for socially and economically better-off sections of society to contribute, in an organised and accountable manner, to ease hardship during colder months. As cold conditions persist, priority should remain on ensuring uninterrupted healthcare services and timely relief for vulnerable communities in the north. Strengthening coordination among health authorities, the local administration and relief agencies will be crucial in the coming days. A predictable seasonal response, rather than reactive measures, would help to protect lives and livelihoods during the winter.

title: State reforms largely left unimplemented
body: MOST of the state reform recommendations put forth by the 11 commissions that the interim government instituted towards the end of 2024 may not be implemented during the tenure of the government, which is nearing an end, with the national elections having been set for February 12. The government on October 3, 2024, set up six commissions on electoral reforms, police administrative reforms, judiciary reforms, anti-corruption reforms, public administration reforms and constitutional reforms. The commissions submitted their recommendations between January 15 and February 5. The government on November 18, 2024, formed five more commissions on reforms in the health sector, local government, labour issues, women’s affairs and the media. The commissions submitted their recommendations between February 22 and May 4. The government on February 13 also formed a commission to forge a national consensus on the recommendations, mainly constitutional and political, with several rounds of dialogue with political parties, that later drafted the July national charter to be put to a referendum on the election day. Whilst some recommendations require constitutional amendments for implementation, others could be effected through legislation. Yet, reforms have made limited progress in implementation, with the stakeholders having been largely disappointed. The year that began with high hopes is, thus, ending on a low note. Whilst a handful of the recommendations have either been implemented or entered the implementation phase, most of them have either been set aside, especially the recommendations of the five commissions instituted later, or have not been properly reckoned with. The chief of the commission on electoral reforms says that only two of the 31 immediately actionable proposals have been acted on. The government has so far executed nine of the 30 recommendations of the commission on judicial reforms. The chief of the commission on anti-corruption reforms says that the ordinance promulgated on the reforms has ignored several major strategic proposals and has excluded a review mechanism that could afford more independence to the Anti-Corruption Commission. The Representation of the People Order, revised on the basis of the recommendations, has failed to bring registered political parties under the Right to Information Act. It has also failed to allow legal action against the Election Commission for the breach of oath. The government has set up the Police Commission, based on the proposals of the commission on police administrative reforms, but it has failed to provide any accountability mechanism for the home affairs ministry. Yet, the chief adviser to the interim government Muhammad Yunus on December 16 said that the government was moving towards a well-governed country with the implementation of wide-ranging reform initiatives. It is, therefore, expected that the political government that would emerge through the national elections in February would act on at least the actionable and meaningful recommendations.

title: Denial, memory and moral imperative of justice
body: HISTORY does not disappear because it makes someone uncomfortable. Numbers can be twisted, facts blurred, genocide softened into ‘excesses,’ but the truth of 1971 remains unyielding. It sits at the core of who we are. What is most alarming today is that denial is no longer only across the border; it is growing within Bangladesh. These are not harmless whispers. They shrink genocide into ‘politics,’ question our martyrs and recycle decade-old narratives that Pakistan has propagated for generations. When Pakistan’s deputy prime minister Ishaq Dar visited Dhaka in 2025 and casually declared that 1971 had been ‘settled long ago,’ it was far more than a diplomatic faux pas. From the standpoint of Pakistan’s official narrative, 1971 is ‘settled.’ In Pakistan’s vocabulary, ‘settled’ does not mean justice. It does not mean acknowledgment. It does not mean apology. It means vague ‘regret for excesses’ and teaching generations that Pakistan was the victim. It is a deliberate attempt to silence Bangladesh’s history, to force us into their moral framework and to make us doubt our truth. They insist that Pakistan owes nothing and continue to press Bangladesh to accept their version of history, to forget and to forgive. Decades later, they still act as if they can dictate how Bangladesh should remember its own liberation, still try to force their interpretation, still attempt to impose the sense of guilt and obedience that they demanded in 1971. The reality is undeniable: 1971 has never been settled. Not in 1974, with the Delhi agreement, which expressed only ‘regret for any excesses that may have been committed,’ a phrase designed to minimise systematic murder and rape, reducing calculated atrocities to the level of minor errors. Not when 195 Pakistani officers accused of war crimes were allowed to walk free instead of facing trial, returning home as heroes. Not when General Pervez Musharraf offered vague sorrow without ever uttering the word that matters: apology. The roots of the genocide are decades deep. In 1952, when Bengalis rose to defend their right to speak in their mother tongue, they were met with bullets. Ayub Khan, in his autobiography Friends Not Masters, mentions the Bengalis as ‘lazy, effeminate, incapable of leadership.’ The words, repeated in bureaucratic halls, justified economic exploitation and political marginalisation. After winning a landslide mandate in the 1970 elections, Sheikh Mujibur Rahman was arrested on March 26, 1971 and accused of being a ‘traitor’ for demanding autonomy for East Pakistan. This label was used to justify the military’s brutal crackdown, suppress Bengali demands for self-governance, and maintain West Pakistan’s control. President Yahya Khan publicly warned that Mujibur Rahman a ‘traitor’ and he ‘might not live,’ as reported in Time Magazine, ‘Pakistan: Mujib’s Secret Trial,’ August 23, 19711, while accusing him of plotting to create a separate country. The demand for autonomy had been formalised in Mujibur Rahman’s 1966 Six-Point Movement, and by December 5, 1969, he openly declared that the independent country would be called Bangladesh, a name unanimously accepted by the all the leaders. This vision was further cemented in his historic March 7 speech, turning the idea of a separate country into a collective demand of the Bengali people. On March 25, 1971, Operation Searchlight began, with Dhaka University being among the first targets. Jagannath Hall and Iqbal Hall (now Zahurul Haq Hall) were attacked and professors, students and intellectuals were systematically killed. Archer Blood, then US consul general in Dhaka, wrote in The Cruel Birth of Bangladesh that fire broke out at ‘Rokeya Hall,’ the girls’ hall and when students tried to escape, the army opened fire. Major general Rao Farman Ali, who was in charge of the killings in Dhaka, wrote in his table diary, as recorded by A Niazi in A Stranger in My Own Country, ‘Green land of East Pakistan will be painted red.’ And, it was, indeed, painted red with the blood of the Bengalis. Rao Farman Ali also explains in The Betrayal of East Pakistan how the killings were carefully planned and carried out. A Time Magazine retrospective later described the violence of 1971 as claiming ‘three million lives’ and displacing about 10 million refugees, highlighting the immense human cost of the war. In Blood and Tears, Qutubuddin Aziz chronicles the systematic terror in East Pakistan: entire families were massacred, villages were burnt and women were abducted and held in military camps as sex slaves. During the war, Pakistani forces, often aided by local collaborators aka ‘Razakars,’ deliberately used rape and torture as weapons of war. Official figures initially estimated 200,000 victims, but research suggests that the number was far higher. Dr Geoffrey Davis estimated 400,000–430,000, scholar Susan Brownmiller cited 200,000– 400,000 and field surveys by Dr MA Hasan indicate nearly 468,000 women were affected. Nilima Ibrahim’s book Ami Birangana Bolchi preserves the voice of these survivors and drama artists have brought their stories to life on stage, using their performances to honour the biranganas and ensure their experiences are not forgotten. In Witness to Surrender, Siddiq Salik recounts the chaos: ‘We were told to kill the Hindus and Kafirs. One day in June, we cordoned a village and were ordered to kill the Kafirs. The women were reciting from the Qura’n, the men holding prayers, but they were unlucky. Our commanding officer ordered us not to waste time.’ President Yahya Khan’s infamous directive, ‘Kill three million of them and the rest will eat out of our hands,’ was not mere rhetoric. This statement, recorded in multiple historical accounts including Blood and Tears and corroborated by Niazi in A Stranger in My Own Country, these were not unfortunate casualties in a civil conflict; this was state-directed genocide, meticulously planned, as the Hamoodur Rahman Commission later detailed in its official report. Books like The Blood Telegram by Gary J Bass reveal the global awareness and complicity surrounding the 1971 atrocities. The United States, under Nixon and Kissinger, chose silence and tacit support for Pakistan, prioritising geopolitics over human life despite warnings of genocide. In Diplomacy, Kissinger frames these events in cold, strategic terms while Christopher Hitchens in The Trial of Henry Kissinger exposes how his obsession with realpolitik allowed him to ignore mass killings and remain complicit in Operation Searchlight, enabling the 1971 genocide in Bangladesh. After the 1971 war, injustice did not end. When Bhutto visited Dhaka in 1974, many Bengalis questioned why he was invited at all given the deep wounds of 1971. During that visit, he went to the National Martyrs’ Memorial but reportedly refused to remove his ‘Mao cap’ and declined to sign the visitors’ book presented to him. Instead, he reacted dismissively, allegedly muttering ‘enough of this nonsense’ and pushing the book aside. For decades, Pakistani textbooks have rewritten history, In there version, India becomes the villain, the Bengalis are depicted as misguided separatists and the army’s brutality is minimised as ‘exaggerated.’ Pakistan positions itself as the victim and Bangladesh as merely a tool in an Indian conspiracy. Our Bir Sreshtha Matiur Rahman sacrificed his life to save innocent Bangladeshis, hijacking a Pakistan Air Force jet and crashing it. Yet, at Masroor Airbase in Karachi, even in death, he was vilified, with engraving at his grave: ‘Idhar so raha hai ek gaddar’ (Here lies a traitor.) Despite his ultimate sacrifice for his country, the Pakistani military sought to erase his heroism and brand him a traitor. in contrast, in front of Rashid Minhas’s grave, the Urdu inscription reads: ‘Frowaje don ki ek fiza me mumin ka nisha aur munafikka nisha, aur Rashid ki shahadat ye hai’ (The signs of a true believer and a hypocrite are distinct, even if they traverse the same land). Rashid’s martyrdom was like a verse by poet Iqbal. Rashid Minhas, a Pakistan Air Force pilot and national hero, died in 1971 while defending his aircraft from being hijacked. Below his grave, a poem by Iqbal in Persian reads: ‘Kurguez ka jaha aur hai, shahi ka jaha aur’ (Even if vultures and hawks roam the same place, their realms are separate). Such a strange world we live in. The denial of the 1971 genocide is no longer only imported it has surfaced within Bangladesh. Since 2024, numerous sculptures and memorials connected to the Liberation War have been demolished, neglected or left in ruins. The Lalmonirhat liberation war mural, which honoured both the 1952 language ovement and the 1971 liberation war, was dismantled; the Barguna Liberation War Museum was looted; and, hundreds of sculptures and relics at the Mujibnagar Memorial Complex were defaced. Across the country, similar acts continue. Alarmingly, some domestic groups continue to echo Pakistan’s narratives, playing down the 1971 genocide, distorting history or using religion to justify atrocities. Even major dates like December 16, which mark Bangladesh’s victory and liberation, are increasingly treated with indifference or misrepresented, nearly 55 years after independence. These groups go further, questioning the legitimacy of the names of martyrs and Biranganas, attempting to rewrite who deserves recognition. Although they claim to represent Islam, parties like Jamaat-e-Islami follow the political ideology of Syed Abul A’la Maududi rather than authentic Islamic principles. They opposed Bangladesh’s independence in 1971 and even today, they continue to do politics in the country, promoting narratives and symbols that undermine the nation’s founding ideals while displaying flags and rhetoric aligned with their past opposition. This hostility is not only ideological but also cultural. In 1971, institutions such as Chhayanaut and Udichi were targeted and vandalised because they opposed Pakistan and upheld secular values. Even now, some factions seek to undermine Bangladesh’s cultural and national identity, opposing secularism, attacking cultural organisations and, even, challenging symbols such as the national anthem, written by Rabindranath Tagore, whom they reject for being Hindu and Indian. Alarmingly, during recent unrest, two newspaper outlets were burnt. The government could have intervened to stop the attacks, but it did not, allowing the destruction and chaos to continue unchecked. The facts are unambiguous. As Witness to Surrender records, Pakistan’s Eastern Command surrendered primarily to the Bangladesh forces, with Indian forces. When the surrender came, every military and paramilitary unit across the country gave up where they stood. It was not only a battlefield defeat for Pakistan, it was a moral reckoning, too. And the world recognised it. India formally acknowledged Bangladesh as an independent state on December 6, 1971, breaking the global silence that Pakistan had tried to maintain. Once that door opened, recognition came from country after country. Within days, nations across Asia, Europe and beyond accepted what Bangladeshis had already written with their blood: a sovereign nation was born. This combination of Pakistan’s surrender to Bangladesh’s forces and the swift international recognition that followed shattered every attempt to portray the war as a misunderstanding or an ‘internal affair.’ It confirmed that Bangladesh had not broken away; Bangladesh had been freed. What makes this internal echo of denial so alarming is how it shifts the narrative away from the victims and towards the perpetrators. The denial persists even though the evidence is overwhelming. The number of people killed, raped and abducted in 1971 has been documented in books and testimonies, with names recorded of those who committed the crimes. Yet, some still choose to question the death toll, even suggesting many victims weren’t victims at all. The historical and moral record is undeniable. Even Pakistan’s own collaborators, who were directly involved in the atrocities, acknowledged these crimes in their own writings. Pakistan’s leading newspaper Dawn carried headlines recognising the brutality of 1971. The full release of the Hamoodur Rahman Commission report further confirms that the violence was systematic and state-directed. Cultural resistance also spoke powerfully to the world: George Harrison, Bob Dylan and Ravi Shankar’s ‘Concert for Bangladesh’ helped to expose the humanitarian catastrophe and raised aid for millions of refugees who had fled to India. The evidence is overwhelming. Pakistan must rise in its parliament and state the truth plainly: in 1971, the Pakistani state committed genocide in East Pakistan and ask for unconditional apology. We will engage with any nation where it serves our people and benefits our economy but never at the expense of our dignity. We will look forward, but not by closing our eyes to the past. Pakistani leaders continue to urge forgiveness, often couched in religious language, telling Bangladeshis to ‘clean the heart’ and let go of the past. But, forgiveness cannot be demanded from those who deny the crimes of genocide or refuse to acknowledge the truth. True reconciliation requires naming the atrocities, recognising the suffering and addressing the economic and moral debts owed. Without this honest acknowledgment, calls to forgive are hollow, and both the victims’ memory and Bangladesh’s rightful claims remain ignored. Kollol Kibria ([email protected]) is an advocate, human rights activist and political analyst.

title: IQ, degrees, scholarship and intellect
body: THIS piece reflects the memorable YouTube video discourse between two prominent Bangladeshi intellectuals, Participant X (hereafter PX) and Participant Y (hereafter PY), on December 14, 2024. Their exchange has stayed with me not merely as an event to recall, but as an intellectual disturbance — one that provokes, persists and demands re-examination. Earlier this week, I revisited the discussion not as a passive listener but as a student of thought, tracing what each mind revealed and where our public discourse still hesitates to proceed. Bangladesh stands once more at a moment of political redefinition. Power is shifting, expectations are rising and accountability is being demanded as never before. At such moments, a nation must ask not only who governs, but who thinks; not only who administers, but who interprets; not only who speaks, but who bears responsibility for what is spoken. The PX–PY encounter is therefore not a relic to archive but an unfinished assignment. Since no comprehensive reconciliation of their contrast has yet emerged, an audacious yet humble attempt feels overdue. PX presents the intellectual as an expansive and democratic identity, open to anyone who engages seriously with ideas, injustice, language or power. Thinking, in his view, is neither the privilege of universities nor the inheritance of elite learning. A farmer contesting land rights, a garment worker demanding dignity, a student activist risking arrest — each participates in the intellectual life of a nation when they confront truth or injustice. Thought, here, is awakening rather than entitlement. This inclusivity is morally attractive and politically necessary in societies long suffocated by credentialism and hierarchy. Yet generosity carries its own risk. A definition stretched too wide may dissolve into vagueness. If reflection alone suffices, then everyone becomes an intellectual, even without civic responsibility, ethical discipline or accountability for consequences. A republic cannot function if every opinion claims equal intellectual status regardless of evidence, integrity or social cost. PX’s openness rightly invites participation, but participation alone cannot be the endpoint. Even a democratic concept of intellect requires a threshold if it is to guide public life meaningfully. It is precisely here that PY enters — not as a challenger to PX but as his necessary complement. He does not close the door; he defines what it means to remain inside. For PY, an intellectual is not authenticated by degrees or pedigree, but by responsibility. Thought must mature into moral consequence. Knowledge without conscience is decoration; eloquence without courage is noise. Intellect, in this framing, is not a posture or possession but a burden of truth, the willingness to speak when speech is unwelcome and to defend justice when silence is safer. The convergence of these positions is profound. PX democratises entry; PY preserves gravity. Together, they offer a demanding synthesis: an intellectual is one who cannot escape the responsibilities of thought. They recognise truth, articulate it honestly and stand by its consequences even when clarity invites discomfort or isolation. Intellect is not something one claims; it is something one bears. This synthesis also clarifies a persistent confusion: the tendency to treat intelligence, academic achievement and intellectual responsibility as interchangeable. They are not. Societies that collapse these distinctions end up celebrating credentials while suffering an absence of ideas. To understand why nations are often rich in degrees yet poor in intellectual leadership, we must draw clear border lines among four distinct categories: intelligence, degrees, scholarship and intellectualism. Intelligence, commonly proxied by IQ, measures cognitive capacities such as logical reasoning, abstraction and processing speed. It reflects how efficiently the brain handles information, not wisdom, judgment, ethical reasoning or courage. A high IQ represents cognitive potential, not moral direction. History offers no shortage of highly intelligent individuals who remained politically silent, socially disengaged or morally indifferent. Intelligence, by itself, is value neutral. Degrees certify completion rather than conviction. They signal passage through an institutional curriculum and competence within a defined framework. Degrees are valuable for transmitting accumulated knowledge and maintaining professional standards, but they do not guarantee intellectual independence or ethical courage. A society can produce thousands of graduates while remaining intellectually impoverished if education is reduced to credential accumulation rather than disciplined inquiry. Scholarship occupies a different plane. A scholar is defined by discipline, requiring sustained training, methodological rigor, respect for evidence and patience. Scholars preserve, refine and expand knowledge within specific fields. Their primary audience is often other specialists, and success is judged by accuracy and contribution rather than public visibility. While a high IQ may help, many outstanding scholars are distinguished not by exceptional intelligence but by exceptional perseverance. Yet scholarships do not automatically produce intellectuals. An intellectual is defined by function. Intellectuals use knowledge to interpret society, connect ideas across disciplines, interrogate power and engage the public sphere. They translate specialised understanding into broader social meaning. Intellectualism begins where knowledge meets moral responsibility. It is therefore incorrect to assume that every scholar is also an intellectual. Many scholars quite legitimately choose to remain within academic boundaries, never engaging publicly with the social or political implications of their work. Such restraint does not diminish their scholarship, but it does limit their intellectual role. Conversely, an intellectual does not need to be a formal scholar. Journalists, essayists, scientists, economists, writers and even activists can function as intellectuals if they engage ideas seriously, respect evidence and accept the risks of public reasoning. IQ fits beneath scholarship and intellectualism, not above them. It is a base capacity, not a defining identity. When societies elevate IQ to a badge of superiority, they drift into technocratic elitism, mistaking cleverness for wisdom and efficiency for conscience. This mindset produces brilliant managers who optimise systems without questioning whom those systems serve — administrators who manage injustice smoothly rather than confront it honestly. The healthiest societies understand the hierarchy clearly. Intelligence enables learning. Degrees certify training. Scholarship structures knowledge. Intellectualism gives knowledge direction. Remove any one of these elements, and the system degrades. Intelligence without discipline becomes clever noise. Degrees without inquiry become hollow badges. Scholarship without public engagement turns inward. Intellectualism without knowledge collapses into opinionated activism. Strength lies in alignment, not substitution. Bangladesh’s post-independence failures cannot be explained solely by regimes or institutions. They reflect the absence of a strong and continuous intellectual conscience capable of shaping public judgment and moral direction. A republic survives not by coercion but by consent, and consent rests on argument, memory and shared narrative. When intellectuals weaken — fragmented, silenced, co-opted or afraid — the public imagination becomes vulnerable to propaganda and revisionism. The 1971 assassination of our brightest minds was not only political slaughter; it was the severing of the national brain stem. Bangladesh still lives with that neurological deficit — reduced memory, reduced interrogation, reduced guidance. A simple formulation captures the difference. Scholars ask whether something is correct. Intellectuals ask what it means. Scholars refine truth within disciplines. Intellectuals translate truth into social understanding. Intelligence may accelerate both processes, but it cannot replace either. So what, then, is an intellectual? After revisiting Youtube video debate, the answer emerges not as a choice between inclusivity and exclusivity but as a fusion of the two. Anyone may rise into thought, regardless of class or profession, but one becomes an intellectual only when thought matures into accountability, clarity and consequence.
