Reliance on unapproved drugs under compassionate use during outbreaks has created a dangerous cycle. In Kerala, which faced its fifth outbreak in six years in 2024, and in Bangladesh’s yearly outbreaks, clinicians often resort to ribavirin or remdesivir despite limited and uncertain evidence. Ribavirin, for instance, may only delay death, according to animal studies and observational human data remain inconclusive. This unstructured use not only leaves clinicians without dependable guidance but also complicates the introduction of new therapies into clinical trials. The authors argue for an urgent shift from reactive improvisation to proactive, evidence-based frameworks grounded in early detection, standardised supportive care and adaptive research designs. Beneath these clinical and epidemiological challenges lies a deeper ecological story. A study titled ‘The Ecology of Nipah Virus in Bangladesh: A Nexus of Land-Use Change and Opportunistic Feeding Behavior in Bats,’ published in Viruses (2021), reveals how centuries of human activity have shaped today’s high-risk landscape. Historical deforestation, intensified under British colonial agricultural expansion, forced Pteropus medius bats to adapt to human-dominated ecosystems. Instead of large, nomadic groups, bats now live in smaller, permanent colonies typically composed of around 150 individuals, often near human settlements. Many remain in the same area for a decade or more, sustained by cultivated food sources. Within this altered ecology, raw date palm sap has become the key point of connection between bats and humans. Bats routinely visit tapped trees at night, contaminating the sap. Historical records show that sap tapping expanded during colonial rule, embedding the practice deeply into local culture. Climate plays a role as well, as colder winters explain 53 per cent of the variation in annual spillovers, likely affecting bat physiology, feeding behaviour and sap properties. Interestingly, the study found no significant seasonal pattern in viral shedding among bats. Instead, spillover seasonality appears driven primarily by human and bat interactions with sap. The study introduces the ‘fission-fusion’ continuum. Bangladesh now reflects a state of permanent ‘fission,’ where small bat colonies persist in fragmented landscapes. Australia’s historical Hendra virus ecology involved ‘fusion,’ large, nomadic bat groups, but as Australia undergoes similar anthropogenic pressures, it may also be shifting toward the Bangladeshi model, increasing spillover risk. The authors warn that reactive outbreak measures such as cutting down roost trees are counterproductive, further stressing bat populations and potentially worsening spillover. The research concludes that today’s spillover conditions were created generations ago and cannot be reversed through emergency interventions alone. Effective long-term solutions must integrate ecological understanding with public health action. Preventing bat access to sap using bamboo skirts, maintaining consistent public education against drinking raw sap, restoring ecosystems by planting native fruit trees, strengthening surveillance in bats, livestock and high-risk human populations are all essential. Long-term studies on bat stress, movement ecology and roost loss remain equally critical. Across global literature, the message is consistent: managing Nipah requires more than medical responses. It demands ecological literacy, stronger hospital infection control, smarter land-use planning, better surveillance at the human-animal-environment interface, increased research funding, and regional collaboration. Preventing future Nipah outbreaks in Bangladesh requires a combined public health, ecological and clinical response that tackles the problem at its root. Reducing bat-human contact must begin with protecting date palm sap collection so that bats cannot access it, and with expanding community awareness about the dangers of drinking raw sap and the lifesaving value of boiling it. Surveillance needs to be strengthened not only among humans but also within bat populations, domestic animals and wildlife to detect spillover early. Hospitals must be equipped with reliable diagnostics, uniform supportive care protocols and rapid reporting mechanisms to identify and manage cases at the earliest stage. Long-term ecological restoration must be prioritised, including planting native fruit trees that provide alternative food sources for bats and reducing their dependence on sap. Clinical management must shift decisively away from reactive compassionate-use practices and toward rigorous, evidence-based research supported by innovative trial designs. Sustained regional cooperation, better information sharing and continuous investment in scientific research are fundamental for understanding Nipah’s behaviour and for developing future medical countermeasures. Above all, Bangladesh must embrace the One Health approach, recognising that human, animal and environmental health are inseparable. Only through coordinated, multisectoral action can we interrupt the spillover pathway, prevent outbreaks and protect communities from this deadly virus. Nafew Sajed Joy is a researcher and writer.

title: Rising stakes of food economy
body: The story of Bangladesh’s food economy is one of cautious optimism. Progress in yields, export rebounds and policy orientation offer reason for confidence, but resilience and inclusion will define success, writes Makhan Lal Dutta ON A humid morning in rural Rangpur, a tractor rattles past a cluster of smallholdings where women sort seed potatoes while a teenager scrolls an app showing market prices. That daily choreography — field, cold-room, truck, market and kitchen — now defines a national story: Bangladesh’s food economy is shifting from subsistence farming toward a complex, market-driven system that must feed 170 million people, support livelihoods and meet export expectations all at once. Agriculture remains central but smaller in gross domestic product terms than it once was; in FY2023–24 the sector accounted for roughly 11–12 per cent of GDP while still employing about 44 per cent of the workforce, a sign of both structural transformation and the persistence of rural dependence on farm incomes. This duality frames the policy debate: how to raise productivity, diversify value chains and create higher-paying agribusiness jobs without displacing the millions who depend on land and labour. Rice still carries symbolic and economic weight — Bangladesh recently crossed the 40-million-tonne mark in rice output, a milestone that underscores gains from improved varieties, irrigation and intensification. Yet the same season showed how climate shocks can erase progress: floods and extreme weather in recent years destroyed significant rice stocks and pushed the government to contemplate imports and emergency measures to stabilise prices. The lesson is stark: production gains must be coupled with resilient storage, diversified cropping and risk management. Commodity exports such as shrimp and frozen fish illustrate the food economy’s promise. The sector has bounced back, with exports showing strong recovery and earning crucial foreign exchange; when standards, testing and private investment align, Bangladeshi processors access lucrative global markets. That commercial success, however, depends on continued improvements in quality control, traceability and cold-chain logistics to meet increasingly strict buyer requirements. A policy ecosystem has emerged to steer this transition. Government strategies — the Agro-Food Processing Promotion Policy and the National Food and Nutrition Security Policy — signal an appetite for value-addition, agro-processing parks and public–private partnerships. These frameworks aim to turn raw output into shelf-stable, higher-value products that can sustain industrial jobs and raise rural incomes, but implementation hinges on financing, land allocation and regulatory clarity. Private sector dynamism is visible in processing plants, cold-store investments and e-commerce platforms that change how people buy food in cities. Startups and established firms are experimenting with farm-to-consumer models, traceability apps and aggregation centres that let smallholders reach urban demand. Yet most small farmers and informal traders remain at the periphery, hampered by limited access to credit, technology and market information; inclusive business models are the missing link for scaled, equitable gains. Infrastructure deficits are a recurring constraint. Poor rural roads, intermittent electricity and narrow cold chains inflate post-harvest losses — estimates suggest food loss across fruits, vegetables and fish erodes both incomes and food availability. Addressing these gaps requires coordinated public investment, concessional finance for cold-chain builders and targeted subsidies that nudge adopters toward mechanised drying, improved packaging and refrigerated transport. Labour and skills matter as the food economy modernises. Agro-processing needs technicians, quality managers and logistics specialists; yet vocational training in these niches is limited. Expanding curricula, apprenticeships and extension services can create career pathways off the farm and into higher-value segments. Such human-capital investments are as vital as roads and refrigerators for a resilient, competitive food sector. Climate change adds urgency and a reshaping force. Heat stress, shifting rainfall and extreme floods are already imposing production costs and health burdens that ripple through supply chains. Building climate-smart agriculture — drought-tolerant seeds, flood-resilient infrastructure, insurance mechanisms — must be part of any food-economy strategy if Bangladesh hopes to safeguard yields and incomes while continuing to export processed goods. For policymakers, the balancing act is clear: pursue productivity and export growth while protecting smallholders and ensuring food security. Practical steps — scaling laboratory testing, linking farmers to processors via contract farming, investing in rural roads and targeted social safety nets — can reinforce each other. The food economy’s future will be decided less by grand plans than by these pragmatic fixes that stitch markets, people and nature into one functioning system. The story of Bangladesh’s food economy is therefore one of cautious optimism. Progress in yields, export rebounds and policy orientation offer reason for confidence, but resilience and inclusion will define success. From the paddy fields to the packed trays of frozen shrimp, the choices made now about investment, skills and climate adaptation will determine whether food becomes a ladder to prosperity or a source of vulnerability for millions. Dr Makhan Lal Dutta, an irrigation engineer, is CEO of Harvesting Knowledge Consultancy.

title: Kosovo votes in bid to break  year-long political deadlock
body: Kosovo citizens are voting Sunday in snap parliamentary elections, hoping to end ten months of political deadlock. Vetevendosje, the party of incumbent prime minister Albin Kurti, won the most votes in last February’s parliamentary elections, but its 42 per cent was not enough to secure a majority in the 120-seat parliament. MPs needed more than 50 sessions to agree on a speaker, but no coalition or government emerged, forcing the country to go back to the polls. By 11:00am local time (10 GMT), 8.27 per cent of citizens had voted, broadly in line with turnout in February, which ended with just 40.6 per cent of voters turning out. Arben Xhelili, 42, an economist from Pristina, was not optimistic after casting his vote. ‘I expect the same situation after the elections,’ he said. Brikenda Rexhepi, editor-in-chief of Koha Media Group, said that ‘beyond political instability and public disappointment, the deadlock has had clear economic and diplomatic costs.’ She said this election offers the opportunity to form ‘functioning institutions after a year of failed attempts’. In front of one of the polling stations in Pristina, Arefik Mexhmejli, a 66-year-old pensioner, said whoever wins ‘should work harder for the economy’. Seen as the frontrunner, Kurti hopes, after a rapid two-week campaign, to ‘win by a wide margin’ and ‘go beyond 50 per cent,’ he said in an interview on Tuesday. While he campaigned in February on a promise to govern Kosovo ‘from one end to the other’ — including Serb-majority areas where Belgrade’s influence often outweighs Pristina’s — Kurti has now focused on the economy, sidelining relations with Serbia—which has never recognised the secession of its former province in 2008. ‘Beyond the controversies, the economy is doing very well and this year again we will record GDP growth of 4 per cent. Throughout my term, we have never fallen below 4 per cent,’ Kurti said. In recent days, he has also announced that the government would pay 100 euros ($117) to pensioners and to every family with young children by the end of the year. ‘Electoral corruption,’ responded the two other main parties, the Democratic Party of Kosovo and the Democratic League of Kosovo. They have also campaigned on the economy and the most vulnerable groups — but by attacking the government record. ‘Kosovo has been poorly governed. Prices have risen by 40 to 50 per cent, electricity has become more expensive, while wages and pensions have remained almost unchanged. That will change with a PDK government,’ promised PDK leader Bedri Hamza. ‘Development projects have never progressed because of poor political choices,’ and ‘inflation has eaten away at incomes,’ echoed Lumir Abdixhiku, the LDK candidate. He criticised Kurti’s hard-line policy towards the Serb minority, which has also been lambasted by allies, including the United States. ‘We have lost allies, we have lost the trust of the international community, institutions have been blocked,’ Abdixhiku accused. More than two million people are eligible to vote — including tens of thousands registered abroad — in Sunday’s election. ‘We expect better than what it is now,’ Suzana Simnica, 53, said after voting in Pristina. High expectations were also voiced by Fatmir Vehapi, 65, who came from Switzerland just to vote. In addition to the three main parties, voters must also choose representatives for the 20 seats reserved for minorities — 10 for the Serb minority, four for Roma, Ashkali and Balkan Egyptians, three for Bosniaks, two for Turks and one for Gorani.

title: Poverty and corruption
body: BANGLADESH today stands trapped inside two interconnected circles, poverty and corruption, like a nation caught on a spinning, grinding wheel. One suffocates households from below, the other hollows out institutions from above; one deprives citizens of nutrition, education, mobility and hope, while the other deprives the state of leadership, trust and moral legitimacy. These are not separate problems running side by side, they mesh like interlocking gears. Poverty breeds vulnerability, corruption breeds impunity, and together they form a twin trap: self-reinforcing, cyclical and clinically insidious. Among everyday citizens, corruption often begins not with greed, but with aspiration. Newly married couples, and those preparing to marry, increasingly pursue an upscale urban life with modern amenities, better schools, safer neighborhoods, mobility and social prestige. But legitimate income rarely matches those ambitions. As the gap between earnings and aspiration widens, temptation enters quietly. Family expectations add fuel: parents want children to rise, spouses expect dignity signaled through comfort and society rewards display over restraint. When income cannot sustain the life one wants to project, ‘small’ acts of under-the-table convenience become rationalised as necessity. A shortcut becomes a habit — and soon, a culture. This form of corruption is distinct from bureaupolitigraft — the structured, large-scale graft produced by political-bureaucratic symbiosis. Bureaupolitigraft feeds on power; aspirational corruption feeds on desire. Both drain national integrity — one systemically, the other socially — but together they build the foundations of a profoundly corrupted state. The coming national election exposes this reality starkly. BNP has nominated 272 candidates, with 28 pending — many of whom are remembered less for service than for scandal, evasion and entitlement. Nominations have quietly transformed from responsibility to investment. Once a nomination is purchased, the office must yield return. Politics imitates venture capital, power becomes an asset class and parliament morphs into a profit hub. Small wonder political neophytes — unqualified even for mid-level civil roles — bid aggressively for candidacy. When office is bought, governance becomes rent-seeking; when power is traded, the public interest is pawned. Many returnees are sexagenarians and septuagenarians who, in their quinquagenarian prime, presided over the years when Bangladesh earned the ignominy of ranking as the most corrupt nation on earth five times consecutively (2001–2006). Their legacy is not a fading scar — it is the architecture of dysfunction we still occupy. Age is no disqualification, but age without evolution becomes entitlement embalmed in decay. The nation watches with uneasy curiosity: will their return repeat the old script in déjà vu — or will it mark a long-delayed moral awakening? Recent nomination behavior suggests little has been learned from the July uprising that sent looters fleeing — homeless, disgraced and slipping across borders under cover of night to evade accountability. Bangladesh cannot afford nostalgia for predators who mistake power for inheritance. Corruption is not merely theft, it is a business model of governance built on extraction. At every civic touchpoint — police clearance, utility connection, land mutation, hospital report, business permit, court affidavit — the citizen pays a toll. Poverty weakens resistance just as corruption strengthens incentive. The poor cannot afford justice; the powerful can purchase impunity. One side submits out of survival, the other abuses out of entitlement, a symbiosis of suffering and plunder that turns rights into privilege and privilege into immunity. A poverty trap means a child born disadvantaged grows into disadvantage — malnourished, unskilled, unseen except as labour. A corruption trap means a citizen seeking fairness must first negotiate power — pay, plead, or perish. One locks the body; the other locks the future. Worse, corruption drains the very resources needed to break poverty: budgets leak, tenders inflate, loans disappear, bridges crack. Each stolen taka births another generation of cheap political muscle, children who grow into men hired for rallies, protection, or violence. Poverty reproduces vulnerability; corruption reproduces dominion. The twin trap does not merely persist, it regenerates. The order of reform matters. Poverty cannot be abolished without income, investment, and mobility. Yet investment withers under uncertainty, growth collapses without trust, and trust cannot survive without rule of law. Rule of law cannot exist where corruption governs. Bangladesh must break the corruption trap first; poverty will not fall while bribery remains the price of participation in civic life. When politics becomes franchise ownership, governance devolves into collection. Ministries convert into private estates, public assets into revenue streams, and the nation runs through intermediaries — brokers, fixers, collectors. Elections may change faces, but systems persist unless incentives change. The electorate now stands at the edge of a historic decision. Will power return to those who normalised plunder, or move to those with intellectual honesty, institutional discipline and administrative courage? On this choice, it rests whether the twin trap tightens, or fractures. Democracy is not merely voting; it is stewardship. It is the resolve to say ‘not again.’ Bangladesh has suffered enough under rulers who treated the treasury like inheritance and citizens like collateral. What the nation needs is not just new rulers, but new thinking. True reform requires institutions that outlast personalities. No country has lifted millions from poverty while treating bribery as an operating cost. Breaking the twin trap requires transformation across three dimensions: politics must move from extraction to service; governance from secrecy to accountability; and the economy from survival to productivity. None is easy, all are indispensable. No society prospers when the honest are punished and the corrupt are promoted; no democracy survives where citizens are valuable only during elections, disposable afterward. Bangladesh is not at a crossroads, it is in a cul-de-sac, unless an exit is carved through walls built by corrupticians and mortgaged on the backs of the poor. History will not forgive another cycle of returnees recycling ruin. This nation deserves leadership capable of rising above appetite, beyond entitlement and outside the closed circle of past predators. Corruption impinges from two channels: low-income public servants and the collusion of bureaucrats and politicians. The diagram, instead of explaining a theory, shows a mechanism. Each box flows logically, exposing how deprivation and dysfunction feed each other like two gears locked into mutual rotation. On the left, poverty reproduces itself economically — low income → low savings → low investment → low productivity → low growth → deeper poverty. On the right, corruption reproduces itself institutionally — weak institutions → weak enforcement → corruption → revenue leakage → low investment → low productivity. The diagram shows how poverty and corruption intersect: low income drives corruption, and corruption depresses income and growth. Public discourse often treats them as separate problems, but here they appear as a single braided trap. The two return arrows close the loop like a feedback circuit, showing the cycle repeating indefinitely unless disrupted. Between poverty and low income, causality is not linear but circular, a chicken-and-egg paradox of development. One may begin with low income and sink into poverty as opportunities contract, savings evaporate, investment shrinks, productivity falls, and growth collapses; or one may be born into poverty itself and inherit deprivation before agency ever arrives. Poverty produces low income, low income deepens poverty, and the loop closes upon itself. Low income can ignite corruption too. When wages cannot sustain a household, when effort brings dignity but not survival, the line between need and transgression blurs. A clerk demands speed money, a police officer accepts a fee for leniency, a bureaucrat delays service until ‘tea money’ flows — desperation masquerading as discretion. Corruption drains revenue, leakage weakens development, investment falls, productivity declines, growth slows and poverty returns to claim another generation. Two traps, two spirals, braided into one. Bangladesh can still break free but only if corruption is treated not as culture but as enemy, not as inconvenience but as existential threat. Dr Abdullah A Dewan is a professor emeritus of economics at Eastern Michigan University, USA.

title: Vigilantism, impunity, worrying crisis of governance
body: THE killing of a Hindu young man and the burning of his body at Bhaluka in Mymensingh on December 18 by an organised mob on allegations that he had hurt religious sentiments once again raises a few serious questions about law and order. The young man, who worked with an apparel factory, was beaten to death by what appears to have been an organised mob, which later took the body to the Dhaka–Mymensingh Highway, where it was burnt. No one until December 19 evening was arrested. Alarming as it is, the incident is by no means isolated. It, rather, reflects the cumulative decline in law and order and the government’s failure to stop such crimes by bringing the perpetrators of earlier incidents to justice. It also exposes the abysmal and worrying build-up of religious fanaticism, which has increasingly become destructive and disruptive. When attacks on individuals or groups of other faiths and ideologies over allegations of hurting religious sentiments occurred in the past, they have only multiplied in recent times. Such fanaticism has grown to the extent that organised mobs even exhumed the body of a Sufi practitioner and burnt it in daylight on September 5. Attacks on Sufi practitioners and their shrines and the government’s failure to prevent them, in fact, remain a major blemish on the interim government, which assumed office on August 8, 2024, after the fall of the Awami League regime on August 5 that year, promising to protect the interests of people of all faiths. Since then, there have been attacks on more than a hundred shrines, cultural and religious sites and dozens of devotees of pirs, fakirs and Sufi Islam across the country, leaving many shrines damaged and many devotees injured. The killing of innocent people or petty thieves by angry mobs has also continued unabated. The most alarming is the inaction or inadequate response of the law enforcement agencies. In many cases, the law enforcement agencies were either slow to react or failed to act decisively to stop the mobs. The failure squarely rests with the government, which has largely limited its response to official statements of condemnation. Part of the responsibility also lies with religious scholars and civil society for not being vocal enough to deter mobs from killing people and vandalising property in the name of religion. The government should acknowledge its failure and make a course correction. A mob culture, fuelled by religious fanaticism, poses a serious threat to democratic ideals. The government should, therefore, bring the perpetrators of the Mymensingh incident to justice. It should also investigate earlier incidents and ensure that justice is served.

title: An attack on media and democratic way of life
body: THE attack on the media that took place for hours beginning late December 18, centring on the death of Sharif Osman Hadi, a noted face of the July 2024 uprising and spokesperson of Inquilab Mancha, is heinous. Osman Hadi died early that night while being treated in Singapore after he had been shot at in Dhaka on December 12. We are much saddened by his murder and, even, angry. We demand once again, as we did on December 14, that the government should immediately investigate the murder in a credible manner and hold the perpetrators to justice. However, we strongly condemn the violent, organised attack on the offices of the Daily Star and Prothom Alo that a large organised group of young people had carried out for several hours cashing in on Osman Hadi’s death. The group stormed the office buildings of the two newspapers, vandalised them and set them on fire. The burning of the Daily Star office, with two dozen and a half members on the staff trapped inside, constitutes a clear case of attempted murder as the attackers also prevented fire engines from reaching the building and firefighters from rescuing the people and putting out the flames. The group also attacked the New Age editor Nurul Kabir, also president of the Editors’ Council, who went there to help expedite rescue efforts. A section of the youth group also vandalised and set fire to Chhayanaut, an institution promoting and practising Bengali culture, at Dhanmondi when the attack on the newspaper offices continued. We see this attack on the media not merely as an attack on the media. This is, rather, an attack on the democratic freedom of speech and expression and the democratic way of life. Because, it involves the interests of the entire society. The condemnation of, resistance against and ensuring steps to stop the recurrence of such attacks are not only the responsibility of the media but also of the entire society. We have seen the government showing a lacklustre attitude towards the attack on the media houses and also the cultural organisation. The law enforcement agencies, despite their presence in front of the two newspaper offices at least, failed to contain the attacks by being adequately active in their response to the situation. We, therefore, demand that the government should immediately carry out the investigations of the attacks, not only the two media houses and Chhayanaut in Dhaka but also the attacks that the group carried out on the Daily Star and Prothom Alo offices in Rajshahi and on Prothom Alo offices in Sylhet, Khulna and Kushtia and ensure the punishment of the attackers. The government should, therefore, shrug off its lacklustre attitude that it has showed and credibly investigate the attacks and ensure their punishment.

title: Rebranding genocide
body: FIRST, it was Israel’s right to defend itself. Then it was a war, even though, by Israel’s own military intelligence database, 83 per cent of the casualties were civilians. The 2.3 million Palestinians in Gaza, living under an Israeli air, land and sea blockade, have no army, air force, no mechanized units, no tanks, no navy, no missiles, no heavy artillery, no fleets of killer drones, no sophisticated tracking systems to map all movements, or an ally like the United States, which has given Israel at least $21.7 billion in military aid since October 7, 2023. Now, it is a ‘ceasefire.’ Except of course, as usual, Israel only abided by the first of the 20 stipulations. It freed around 2,000 Palestinian captives held in Israeli prisons — 1700 of whom were detained after October 7 — as well as around 300 bodies of Palestinians, in exchange for the return of the 20 remaining Israeli captives. Israel has violated every other condition. It has tossed the agreement — brokered by the Trump administration without Palestinian participation — into the bonfire with all the other agreements and peace accords concerning Palestinians. Israel’s extensive and blatant flouting of international agreements and international law — Israel and its allies refuse to abide by three sets of legally binding orders by the International Court of Justice (ICJ) and two ICJ advisory opinions, as well as the Genocide Convention and international humanitarian law — presage a world where the law is whatever the most militarily advanced countries say it is. The sham peace plan — ‘President Donald J Trump’s Comprehensive Plan to End the Gaza Conflict’ — in an act of stunning betrayal of the Palestinian people, was endorsed by most of the UN Security Council in November, with China and Russia abstaining. Member states washed their hands of Gaza and turned their backs on the genocide. The adoption of resolution 2803 (2025), as the Middle East scholar Norman Finkelstein writes, ‘was simultaneously a revelation of moral insolvency and a declaration of war against Gaza. By proclaiming international law null and void, the Security Council proclaimed itself null and void. Vis-à-vis Gaza, the Council transmuted into a criminal conspiracy.’ The next phase is supposed to see Hamas surrender its weapons and Israel withdraw from Gaza. But these two steps will never happen. Hamas — along with other Palestinian factions — reject the Security Council resolution. They say they will disarm only when the occupation ends and a Palestinian state is created. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has vowed that if Hamas does not disarm, it will be done ‘the hard way.’ The ‘Board of Peace,’ headed by Trump, will ostensibly govern Gaza along with armed mercenaries from the Israel-allied International Stabilization Force, although no country seems anxious to commit their troops. Trump promises a Gaza Riviera that will function as a ‘special economic zone’ — a territory operating outside of state law governed entirely by private investors, such as the Peter Thiel-backed charter city in Honduras. This will be achieved through the ‘voluntary’ relocation of Palestinians — with those fortunate enough to own land offered digital tokens in exchange. Trump declares that the US ‘will take over the Gaza Strip’ and ‘own it.’ It is a return to the rule of viceroys — though apparently not the odious Tony Blair. Palestinians, in one of the most laughable points in the plan, will be ‘deradicalized’ by their new colonial masters. But these fantasies will never come to fruition. Israel knows what it wants to do in Gaza and it knows no nation will intercede. Palestinians will struggle to survive in primitive and dehumanizing conditions. They will, as they have so many times in the past, be betrayed. Israel has committed 738 violations of the ceasefire agreement between October 10 and December 12, including 358 land and air bombardments, the killing of at least 383 Palestinians and the injuring of 1,002 others, according to the Government Media Office in Gaza and the Palestinian Health Ministry. That’s an average of six Palestinians killed daily in Gaza — down from an average of 250 a day before the ‘ceasefire.’ Israel said it killed a senior Hamas commander, Raed Saad, on Saturday, in a missile strike on a car on Gaza’s coastal road. Three others were also apparently killed in the strike. The genocide is not over. Yes, the pace has slowed. But the intent remains unchanged. It is slow motion killing. The daily numbers of dead and wounded — with increasing numbers falling sick and dying from the cold and rain — are not in the hundreds but the dozens. December saw an average of 140 aid trucks allowed into Gaza each day — instead of the promised 600 — to keep Palestinians on the edge of famine and ensure widespread malnutrition. In October, some 9,300 children in Gaza under five were diagnosed with severe acute malnutrition, according to UNICEF. Israel has opened the border crossing into Egypt at Rafah, but only for Palestinians leaving Gaza. It is not open for those who want to return to Gaza, as stipulated in the agreement. Israel has seized some 58 per cent of Gaza and is steadily moving its demarcation line — known as ‘the yellow line’ — to expand its occupation. Palestinians who cross this arbitrary line — which constantly shifts and is poorly marked when it is marked at all — are shot dead or blown up — even if they are children. Palestinians are being crammed into a shrinking, fetid, overcrowded concentration camp until they can be deported. About 92 per cent of Gaza’s residential buildings have been damaged or destroyed and around 81 per cent of all structures are damaged, according to UN estimates. The Strip, only 25 miles long and seven-and-a-half miles wide, has been reduced to 61 million tons of rubble, including nine million tons of hazardous waste that includes asbestos, industrial waste, and heavy metals, in addition to unexploded ordnance and an estimated 10,000 decaying corpses. There is almost no clean water, electricity or sewage treatment. Israel blocks shipments of construction supplies, including cement and steel, shelter materials, water infrastructure and fuel, so nothing can be rebuilt. Eighty-two per cent of Israeli Jews support the ethnic cleansing of the entire population of Gaza and 47 per cent support killing all civilians in cities captured by the Israeli military. Fifty-nine per cent support doing the same to Palestinian citizens of Israel. Seventy-nine per cent of Israeli Jews say they are ‘not so troubled’ or ‘not troubled at all’ by reports of famine and suffering among the population in Gaza, according to a survey conducted in July. The words ‘Erase Gaza’ appeared more than 18,000 times in Hebrew-language Facebook posts in 2024 alone, according to a new report on hate speech and incitement against Palestinians. The newest form of genocidal celebration in Israel — where social media and news channels routinely chortle over the suffering of Palestinians — is the sprouting of golden nooses on the lapels of members of the far-right political party Otzma Yehudit, Israel’s version of the Ku Klux Klan, including one worn by National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir. They are pushing a bill through the Knesset which seeks to mandate the death penalty for Palestinians who ‘intentionally or indifferently causes the death of an Israeli citizen,’ if they are said to be motivated by ‘racism or hostility toward a public,’ and with the purpose of harming the Israeli state or ‘the rebirth of the Jewish people in its land,’ the Israeli human rights group Adalah explains. More than 100 Palestinians have been killed in Israeli jails since October 7. If the new bill becomes law — it has been cleared through its first reading — it will join the wave of more than 30 anti-Palestinian laws enacted since October 7. The message the genocide sends to the rest of the world, more than a billion of whom live on less than a dollar a day, is unequivocable: We have everything and if you try and take it away from us, we will kill you. This is the new world order. It will look like Gaza. Concentration camps. Starvation. Obliteration of infrastructure and civil society. Mass killing. Wholesale surveillance. Executions. Torture, including the beatings, electrocutions, waterboarding, rape, public humiliation, deprivation of food and denial of medical care routinely used on Palestinians in Israeli prisons. Epidemics. Disease. Mass graves where corpses are bulldozed into unmarked pits and where bodies, as in Gaza, are dug up and torn apart by packs of ravenous wild dogs. We are not destined for the Shangri-La sold to a gullible public by fatuous academics such as Stephen Pinker. We are destined for extinction. Not only individual extinction — which our consumer society furiously attempts to hide by peddling the fantasy of eternal youth — but wholesale extinction as temperatures rise to make the globe uninhabitable. If you think the human species will respond rationally to the ecocide, you are woefully out of touch with human nature. You need to study Gaza. And history. If you live in the Global North, you will get to peer out at the horror, but slowly this horror, as the climate breaks down, will migrate home, turning most of us into Palestinians. Given our complicity in the genocide, it is what we deserve. Empires, when they feel threatened, always embrace the instrument of genocide. Ask the victims of the Spanish conquistadors. Ask Native Americans. Ask the Herero and Nama. Ask the Armenians. Ask the survivors of Hiroshima or Nagasaki. Ask the Indians who survived the Bengal famine or the Kikuyu who rose against their British colonizers in Kenya. Climate refugees will get their turn. This is not the end of the nightmare. It is the beginning. ScheerPost.com, December 16. Chris Hedges is a Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist who was a foreign correspondent for fifteen years for The New York Times, where he served as the Middle East Bureau Chief and Balkan Bureau Chief for the paper. He is the host of show The Chris Hedges Report.

title: Innovation-led education
body: REAL progress is never accidental; it is driven by societies courageous enough to adapt, to harness technology and to make innovation a way of life. These are the undeniable engines of modern economic growth. Conversely, when change is ignored and industries cling to the past, stagnation is inevitable. At the heart of this dynamic lies education, the bedrock of human capital. An economy and its education system are not just linked; they are two sides of the same coin. The awarding of the 2025 Nobel Prize in Economics to Joel Mokyr, Philippe Aghion and Peter Howitt reinforces this fundamental truth. Their collective research demonstrates that sustained prosperity springs from a society’s willingness to embrace ‘creative destruction’, the continuous cycle where outdated systems are replaced by more productive ones. Economies thrive not by preserving the status quo, but when innovation actively challenges it. We need only look at how technology-driven giants like Amazon and Uber redefined entire markets. Here in Bangladesh, we are witnessing our own wave of transformation. From digital banking and e-commerce to tech-based delivery and ride-sharing services, homegrown ventures are rewriting traditional business models, creating new opportunities and driving growth through what was once dismissed as disruptive chaos. The laureates’ work offers a crucial warning: overprotecting established industries may offer short-term stability but stifles dynamism. Sustained innovation, the laureates argue, requires an ecosystem that ensures fair competition, inclusive education and robust social safety nets. In essence, economic growth and social inclusion must advance hand in hand. Mokyr, Aghion and Howitt remind us that every industrial revolution has been propelled by the interaction between scientific understanding and practical know-how, not by chance, but through deliberate investment in knowledge and skills. Their theory of ‘innovation-led growth’ shows that economies advance when firms continually climb a ‘quality ladder,’ creating new products and processes that render old ones obsolete. To sustain this creative cycle, education systems cannot remain static. Policymakers and academic institutions must rethink curricula, pedagogy and skill development models to prepare learners for constant technological renewal. If existing systems are protected too rigidly, creativity suffocates; yet without protecting innovators, the drive to discover fades. The challenge lies in striking the right balances, encouraging competition and invention while equipping people through education to thrive in an ever-evolving world. Understanding the nature of the Fourth Industrial Revolution is crucial in this context. Unlike previous revolutions, the 4IR is not just about technological progress, it represents a convergence of the physical, digital and biological worlds. This fusion has blurred disciplinary boundaries, demanding collaboration across science, design, technology, and the humanities. Today’s industries rely on automation, robotics, data analytics, the Internet of Things and Artificial Intelligence. But the real challenge lies in preparing a workforce capable of adapting creatively within this complex ecosystem. In the 4IR era, jobs evolve overnight and skills quickly become obsolete. A system designed merely to measure pre-determined outcomes now feels like a straitjacket. Can education built for the known truly prepare learners for a future defined by the unknown? To meet this challenge, our educational philosophy must shift decisively from memorisation to adaptive, inquiry-based learning. The critical skills for the 4IR — creativity, critical thinking, collaboration and ethical reasoning — demand a multidisciplinary approach to teaching and learning. For Bangladesh, this means rethinking how education and training can nurture innovation, adaptability and agility in the workforce. A multidisciplinary model is not a luxury but a necessity to build professionals capable of working across diverse fields and contributing meaningfully to a rapidly changing global economy. The message from this year’s Nobel laureates is both urgent and transformative for Bangladesh. Our universities and technical institutions still emphasise routine learning and credentialing over creativity and problem-solving. To sustain long-term growth, Bangladesh must cultivate a generation capable of climbing the quality ladder described by Aghion and Howitt — individuals who can question, experiment, and innovate rather than merely replicate. This calls for bold reforms in curricula, assessment and teacher development, linking education more closely with research, technology and industry. An innovation-driven economy cannot be built on outdated pedagogies. It requires a learning ecosystem that values adaptability and continuous renewal. The choice before us is clear: we can either be passive witnesses to change, or we can be its architects. By embracing the lessons of creative destruction and re-engineering our educational foundation, we can transform our immense demographic dividend into a sustained engine of inclusive and sustainable growth for Bangladesh. MM Shahidul Hassan is a distinguished professor at the Eastern University and former vice-chancellor of the East West University.

title: Human dignity in prisons
body: BANGLADESH’S ratification of the Optional Protocol to the Convention Against Torture marks an important step in its commitment to upholding international rights standards, especially regarding the treatment of persons deprived of liberty. The convention requires all state parties to establish a national preventive mechanism, an independent body tasked with conducting regular, proactive visits to places of detention, including prisons, to prevent torture and other cruel, inhuman, or degrading treatment or punishment. This obligation is now operationalised domestically through the empowerment of the National Human Rights Commission, with legal authority to inspect detention facilities independently. As Bangladesh begins implementing this mandate, the challenge ahead is not just legal compliance but building a competent, effective and sustainable national preventive mechanism that can meaningfully improve prison conditions and uphold human dignity. Clear legal and institutional frameworks: A competent national preventive mechanism must rest on a solid legal foundation. The convention and its implementation guidelines emphasise that the national preventive mechanism’s mandate, powers, composition and independence should be clearly established in law or formal regulations, ensuring that it can operate without undue interference. For Bangladesh, the recent National Human Rights Commission Ordinance 2025, which designates the commission as the national preventive mechanism, is an essential first step. However, further legislative refinement may be necessary to clarify the mechanism’s scope such as specifying the range of places of detention it can visit (beyond prisons to include police custody, immigration detention, and psychiatric facilities), the mechanism’s unhindered access rights, and its authority to interview detained persons privately and obtain relevant information and documentation. These provisions are critical because the primary preventive function of the mechanism is predicated on unfettered access to locations and individuals, so that systemic risks can be identified and addressed. Functional independence and adequate resources: Independence is a cornerstone of any effective monitoring body. Under the convention, state parties must guarantee the functional independence of the mechanism in law and practice, free of political or administrative pressure. This means that the mechanism should have its own budgetary autonomy, authority to recruit staff and freedom to publish reports without censorship. Practical steps include establishing the national preventive mechanism as a separate unit within the commission with its own personnel and budget line and mandating fixed terms and transparent appointment procedures for its members to shield them from arbitrary dismissal. Financial autonomy is crucial because without adequate funding, even well-intentioned institutions cannot develop internal capacity, conduct thorough visits, or follow up on recommendations. Furthermore, high-level political support, coupled with safeguards against interference, will help to build public confidence and deter reprisals against staff or informants participating in monitoring activities. A clear mandate that explicitly prohibits sanctions for those engaging with the mechanism, including prison staff and detainees, can reassure stakeholders that the process is protective rather than punitive. Skilled, multidisciplinary team: A core determinant of the effectiveness of a national preventive mechanism is the competence, independence and professionalism of its personnel. Monitoring prisons and other places of detention is a complex task that requires multidisciplinary expertise as detainees often experience intersecting legal, physical, psychological and social vulnerabilities. Effective preventive monitoring therefore depends on teams with backgrounds in law enforcement, public health, psychiatry, psychology, social work, human rights law and criminology. As emphasised by organisations such as Dignity, the Danish Institute Against Torture, access to detention facilities alone is insufficient. Monitors must also be equipped to document risks, identify patterns of ill-treatment and engage ethically and sensitively with detainees. Robust monitoring tools, along with training in ethical screening, documentation and trauma-informed approaches, are essential to preventing torture and ill-treatment. In Bangladesh, the national commission, as the designated or prospective mechanism, must place strategic recruitment and systematic capacity-building at the centre of its institutional development. This requires structured training programmes aligned with the preventive mandate of the convention, focusing on risk identification rather than individual complaint investigation. Staff should be trained in international human rights law and UN standards such as the Nelson Mandela and Bangkok Rules, alongside practical skills in confidential interviewing, detention analysis, and evidence-based reporting. Partnerships with experienced actors like Dignity and the UN subcommittee on prevention of torture, complemented by national civil society expertise, would strengthen the mechanism’s credibility and support a shift from episodic oversight toward sustained, systemic prevention. Clear monitoring procedures and tools: Competent prison monitoring requires standardised procedures and tools that guide inspectors on how to conduct visits, document conditions, and evaluate compliance with human rights norms. The convention implementation guides recommend adopting protocols that spell out how to examine material conditions, health services, use of restraints, and general treatment of detainees. Bangladesh’s mechanism should develop a country-specific monitoring toolkit that includes checklists, interview guides, health assessment criteria and reporting templates. These tools should draw on international standards while being contextualized to local conditions. For instance, health monitoring tools developed by experts like Dignity can help inspectors assess facilities from a health and dignity perspective, identifying poor nutrition, lack of ventilation, or harmful disciplinary practices. Additionally, the mechanism should institutionalise data management systems to track trends across facilities over time and facilitate the early detection of systemic problems. This could involve digital platforms where inspectors upload reports, record findings and monitor follow-up actions by prison authorities. Establishing a risk assessment framework that maps high-risk facilities and populations (such as juveniles or persons with mental disabilities) will help prioritize resources and tailor interventions. Regular visits and follow-up mechanisms: The proactive nature of the convention requires that mechanisms conduct regular, unannounced visits to prisons and other detention settings. These visits should not be one-off exercises but part of a structured visiting program that covers all relevant institutions within a defined time frame, ensuring continuity and sustained oversight. This approach helps to capture patterns of ill-treatment, identify deterioration in conditions, and enable longitudinal tracking of progress. After each visit, the mechanism must be able to issue recommendations to authorities, such as the home affairs ministry, prisons administrations or the parliament, on how to improve conditions and reduce the risk of torture or abuse. While these recommendations are non-binding under the convention, effective mechanisms secure formal dialogue mechanisms with government counterparts to follow up on implementation. Public reporting, including the publication of annual reports, is another important accountability tool. Reports should be disseminated widely and presented to the parliament or relevant oversight bodies to foster transparency and legislative engagement. Public awareness can also be raised through targeted outreach campaigns explaining the mechanism’s role, detainees’ rights and the importance of humane treatment behind bars. Civil society and public awareness: National preventive mechanisms do not operate in isolation. International guidance encourages meaningful dialogue and cooperation between mechanisms, civil society organisations, academics and other rights defenders. Civil society involvement enhances the mechanism’s legitimacy, amplifies its findings, and strengthens public understanding of torture prevention. In Bangladesh, the mechanism should establish formal partnerships with non-governmental organisations, legal aid clinics, human rights networks and university law clinics. These partnerships can help in gathering documentation, facilitating community outreach, and supporting detainee interviews. Workshops, public seminars and media engagement on the convention and the mechanism’s work can build societal consensus around the need for humane treatment in detention and encourage reporting of abuses. International cooperation and learning: Bangladesh’s mechanism can also benefit from international cooperation with other national mechanisms and the UN subcommittee on prevention of torture, which provides advisory services and technical assistance. Networking with established mechanisms in other countries, such as those in Europe or Asia, can offer insights into best practices, joint training modules, and shared experiences in operational challenges. Such cooperation should extend to participation in regional forums, conferences, and mutual learning platforms, where contexts and strategies are compared and collective innovations are discussed. These international engagements reinforce Bangladesh’s commitment to global human rights norms and integrate the mechanism into a broader global prevention community. Bangladesh’s journey to implement the convention Against Torture presents an opportunity to strengthen rights protection for people deprived of liberty and to embed a culture of prevention, dignity and accountability within its justice system. Establishing a competent national preventive mechanism requires not only legal designation but sustained investment in independence, expertise, monitoring infrastructure, public engagement and international cooperation. By building a well-resourced, autonomous, skilled and collaborative mechanism that conducts regular visits, formulates persuasive recommendations and engages civil society and authorities in meaningful dialogue, Bangladesh can not only meet its international obligations but also profoundly improve the conditions and treatment of detainees in its prisons and other places of custody. This preventive framework, rooted in transparency, respect for human dignity and robust oversight, will not only deter torture and ill-treatment but also strengthen the rule of law and rights culture. Musharraf Tansen is a development analyst and former country representative of the Malala Fund.

title: Attached wealth should serve public interest
body: WHILE the government’s efforts to repatriate ill-gotten, syphoned-off wealth from abroad have made only limited headway in more than 16 months, the authorities attaching and freezing moveable and immoveable assets worth Tk 66,146 crore at home and overseas sends out a signal that impunity is no longer guaranteed. About $16 billion was syphoned out during the Awami League’s 16 years’ regime. The government has so far attached assets valued at Tk 55,638 crore at home and Tk 10,508 crore abroad, according to the national coordination committee, which is tasked with formulating and implementing policies to combat money laundering. Attachment and freezing, however, are merely first steps. What matters now is transparency, stewardship and outcomes: how the assets are managed and how the public interest is safeguarded. The government owes citizens a regular account of how these assets are maintained. Are they under professional management? Are revenues, rents and dividends properly recorded and audited? Without disclosure, attachment risks giving way to quiet decay, with productive assets losing value and public confidence steadily eroding. Transparency in management is, therefore, not optional. It is essential to ensure that attached wealth does not become stranded or quietly dissipated through neglect or mismanagement. Employment-generating assets require particular attention. Factories, mills, logistics facilities and service firms linked to accused individuals or groups should not be shuttered simply because ownership is under investigation. Closure would punish workers, suppliers and local economies rather than those alleged to have been engaged in wrongdoing. The state has the responsibility to keep such enterprises operating through court-appointed administrators, interim boards or trustee arrangements that prioritise continuity. Keeping businesses running preserves value, protects jobs and ensures that the assets transferred to the state, if confiscation is ultimately confirmed, are viable rather than hollowed-out shells. Equally important is clarity over the use of income generated from attached assets. International best practice suggests that such proceeds should be ring-fenced, transparently audited and earmarked for public purposes, whether strengthening the financial system, supporting social protection or offsetting recovery costs. The authorities should also accelerate efforts to recover stolen assets from abroad. At a review meeting on December 17, the coordination committee directed relevant agencies to submit charge sheets as swiftly as possible in all priority cases. Yet, only 14 charge sheets have so far been filed out of 104 priority cases. The government should, therefore, formulate and publish rules, alongside regular disclosures, on the management and the use of attached assets. At the same time, it should consistently pursue every legal avenue to repatriate stolen wealth held overseas. This is a painstaking, time-consuming and costly process. But the frameworks already exist and the government needs to deploy them with determination, strategic focus and sustained diplomacy.

title: Right-wing liberation war talk revisionism poses concern
body: THIS is disparaging that the right-wing Bangladesh Jamaat-e-Islami, which actively opposed Bangladesh’s war for national independence in 1971, and other groups supportive of the political party have reared their head enough to distort the history of the birth of the country, which came about in a bloodied people’s war that spanned nine months. Jamaat and its student wing Islami Chhatra Shibir, known as Islami Chhatra Sangha during the Pakistan days, have not stopped making such a noise in the month of December and, even, on December 16, when the Pakistani forces surrendered to the General Officer Commanding in Chief of the India and Bangladesh Forces in Dhaka. Jamaat and the Islami Chhatra Shibir have propagated a narrative of the war that supports Pakistan and India’s view of the war. The narrative that this was solely a war between Pakistan and India well contradicts what happened in 1971 and belittles the active aspirations of the people of Bangladesh who wanted to break free of repression by the ruling elite of the time nestled in West Pakistan. This, thus, constitutes an insult to the freedom fighters of Bangladesh who laid down their lives for independence and casts an aspersion on the people who wanted to become independent. The Bangladesh Jamaat-e-Islami and the Islami Chhatra Shibir are have engaged in clashes with nationalist forces at places during the celebrations of Victory Day, primarily belittling Bangladesh’s war for independence. A fire is reported to have been set to a grave of a freedom fighter, Abdul Mannan Khan, at Niamatpur in the Shariatpur district headquarters on Victory Day. Fifteen people were injured in a scuffle during the Victory Day celebrations at the Amir Jang Gaznabi Stadium in Bhola after Bangladesh Nationalist Party activists called Jamaat leaders ‘razakars,’ a term generally used to describe the people who collaborated with the killer Pakistani junta during the independence war. Islami Chhatra Shibir activists engaged in a scuffle on the University of Chittagong campus when the Jatiyatabadi Chhatra Dal, the student wing of the Bangladesh Nationalist Party, reached there in a procession to protest against a remark in which the vice-chancellor on December 14, Martyred Intellectuals’ Day, said that it was ‘absurd’ that the Pakistani forces had killed intellectuals during the fag end of the liberation war. Tension brewed up at Jagannath University on Victory day, centring on Pakistan’s national flag being painted on a campus road. The situation worsened as a bus carrying students headed for the National Martyrs’ Memorial and it was prevented from leaving the campus. The Jamaat-e-Islami and like-minded political groups propagating Indian and Pakistani narratives of the Bangladesh war borders on sedition. Yet, what is overwhelming is the silence of the interim government of Muhammad Yunus about the issue. The government must take it up seriously and act accordingly.

title: A better Sri Lanka for all
body: THE Sri Lankan government is rebuilding the cyclone-devastated lives, livelihood and infrastructure in the country after the immense destruction caused by Cyclone Ditwah. The president Anura Kumara Dissanayake is providing exceptional leadership by going into the cyclone affected communities in person, to mingle directly with the people there and to offer encouragement and hope to them. A president who can be in the midst of people when they are suffering and in sorrow is a true leader. In a political culture where leaders have often been distant from the everyday hardships of ordinary people, this visible presence would have a reassuring psychological effect. The international community appears to be comfortable with the government and has been united in giving it immediate support. Whether it be Indian and US helicopters that provided essential airlift capacity or cargo loads of relief material that have come from numerous countries, or funds raised from the people of tiny Maldives, the support has given Sri Lankans the sense of being a part of the world family. The speed and breadth of this response has contrasted sharply with the isolation Sri Lanka experienced during some of the darker moments of its recent past. There is no better indicator of the international goodwill to Sri Lanka as in the personal donations for emergency relief that have been made by members of the diplomatic corps in Sri Lanka. Such gestures go beyond formal diplomacy and suggest a degree of personal confidence in the direction in which the country is moving. The office of the UN representative in Sri Lanka has now taken the initiative to launch a campaign for longer term support, signalling that emergency assistance can be a bridge to sustained engagement rather than a one-off intervention. Balanced statement IN A world that has turned increasingly to looking after narrow national interests rather than broad common interests, Sri Lanka appears to have found a way to obtain the support of all countries. It has received support from countries that are openly rivals to each other. This rare convergence reflects a perception that Sri Lanka is not seeking to play one power against another, and balancing them, but rather to rebuild itself on the basis of stability, inclusiveness and responsible governance. An excerpt from an interview that president Dissanayake gave to the US-based Newsweek magazine is worth reproducing. In just one paragraph, he has summed up Sri Lankan foreign policy that can last the test of time. A question Newsweek put to the president was: ‘Sri Lanka sits at the crossroads of Chinese built infrastructure, Indian regional influence and US economic leverage. To what extent does Sri Lanka truly retain strategic autonomy, and how do you balance these relationships?’ The president replied: ‘India is Sri Lanka’s closest neighbour, separated by about 24km of ocean. We have a civilisational connection with India. There is hardly any aspect of life in Sri Lanka that is not connected to India in some way or another. India has been the first responder whenever Sri Lanka has faced difficulty. India is also our largest trading partner, our largest source of tourism and a significant investor in Sri Lanka. China is also a close and strategic partner. We have a long historic relationship—both at the state level and at a political party level. Our trade, investment and infrastructure partnership is very strong. The United States and Sri Lanka also have deep and multifaceted ties. The US is our largest market. We also have shared democratic values and a commitment to a rules-based order. We don’t look at our relations with these important countries as balancing. Each of our relationships is important to us. We work with everyone, but always with a single purpose – a better world for Sri Lankans, in a better world for all.’ Wider issues THE president’s articulation of foreign relations, especially the underlying theme of working with everyone for the well-being of all, resonates strongly in the context of the present crisis. The willingness of all major partners to assist Sri Lanka simultaneously suggests that goodwill generated through effective disaster response can translate into broader political and diplomatic space. Within the country, the government has been successful in calling for and in obtaining the support of civil society which has an ethos of filling in gaps by seeking the inclusion of marginalised groups and communities who may be left out of the mainstream of development. Civil society organisations have historically played a crucial role in Sri Lanka during times of crisis, often reaching communities that state institutions struggle to access. Following a meeting with CSOs, at which the president requested their support and assured them of their freedom to choose, the CSOs mobilised in all flood affected parts of the country, many of them as part of a CSO Collective for Emergency Response. An important initiative was to undertake the task of ascertaining the needs of the cyclone affected people. Volunteers from a number of civil society groups fanned out throughout the country to collect the necessary information. This effort helped to ground relief efforts in real needs rather than assumptions, reducing duplication and ensuring that assistance reached those most affected. The priority that the government is currently having to give to post-cyclone rebuilding must not distract it from giving priority attention to dealing with postwar issues. The government has the ability and value system to resolve other national problems. Resolving issues of post disaster rebuilding in the aftermath of the cyclone have commonalities in relation to the civil war that ended in 2009. The failure of successive governments to address those issues has prompted the international community to continuously question and find fault with Sri Lanka at the United Nations. This history has weighed heavily on Sri Lanka’s international standing and has limited its ability to fully leverage external support. Required urgency AT A time when the international community is demonstrating enormous goodwill to Sri Lanka, the lessons learnt from their own experiences and the encouraging support they are giving Sri Lanka at present, can and must be utilised. The government under president Dissanayake has committed to a non-racist Sri Lanka in which all citizens will be treated equally. The experience of other countries, such as the United Kingdom, India, Switzerland, Canada and South Africa show that problems between ethnic communities also require inter community power sharing in the form of the devolution of power. Countries that have succeeded in reconciling diversity with unity have done so by embedding inclusion into governance structures rather than treating it as a temporary concession. Sri Lanka’s present moment of international goodwill provides a rare opening to learn from these experiences with the encouragement and support of its partners, including civil society which has shown its readiness to join hands with the government in working for the people’s well-being. The unresolved problems of land resettlement, compensation for lost lives and homes, finding the truth about missing persons continue to weigh heavily on the minds and psyche of people in the former war zones of the north and east even as they do so for the more recent victims of the cyclone. Unresolved grievances do not disappear with time. They resurface periodically, often in moments of political transition or social stress, undermining national cohesion. The government needs to ensure sustainable solutions not only to climate related development, but also to ethnic peace and national reconciliation. The government needs to bring together the urgency of disaster recovery with the long-postponed task of political reform as done in the Indonesian province of Aceh in the aftermath of the 2004 tsunami for which it needs bipartisan political support. Doing so could transform a national tragedy into a turning point for long lasting unity and economic take-off. Jehan Perera is executive director of the National Peace Council of Sri Lanka.

title: Can miracle be revived?
body: AFTER years of rapid growth, Bangladesh confronts inflation, an investment drought, climate shocks and political uncertainty. Its next moves will decide whether its past momentum returns or slips away. In more than a decade, Bangladesh has often been welcomed as a development superstar: steady GDP gains, rising incomes, improvements in health and education and a booming apparel sector. But in the 2024–25 financial year, the picture has become complicated. Inflation is biting, investment has dried up and growth has been revised sharply down. As the nation stands at a crossroads, whether it regains its former trajectory depends on bold reforms and resilient leadership or it risks settling for slower growth in a more fragile economy. Growth slowing FROM 2010 through much of the early 2020s, the economy expanded annually at rates between 6 per cent and 8 per cent. That growth was driven by exports, especially apparel, high remittance inflows, domestic consumption and steadily improving infrastructure. Yet, according to the World Bank’s latest Bangladesh Development Update, the real growth of gross domestic product dropped from 5.8 per cent in the 2023 financial year to 4.2 per cent in the 2024 financial year as both public and private investment softened. For the 2025 financial year, the outlook is more subdued. The Asian Development Bank forecasts growth of 3.9 per cent while the World Bank has slashed its projection to 3.3 per cent, citing elevated inflation, political uncertainty, weak investment and external pressures. Inflation, pressure and invisible costs INFLATION remains a defining concern. In the 2024 financial year, inflation averaged around 9.7 per cent, rising to about 10.2 per cent as projected for the 2025 financial year by the Asian Development Bank. Food and energy prices are particularly volatile, and the depreciation of the taka has mounted pressure on imported inputs. But beyond headline inflation lie hidden costs. A recent World Bank report estimates that rising heat in 2024 cost Bangladesh $1.78 billion, roughly 0.4 per cent of gross domestic product, because of lost workdays, health issues and diminished productivity. Nor is inflation the only invisible scar: weak financial sector health, rising non-performing loans and external sector vulnerabilities are lurking risks. An academic study measuring financial stability found that while the real and fiscal sectors have shown modest improvement, the financial, monetary and external sectors remain the biggest sources of instability. Projections and warnings OPTIMISM surfaces in forecasts for the 2026 financial year. The International Monetary Fund projects a rebound to 6.5 per cent GDP growth alongside an easing of inflation to about 5.2 per cent. The Asian Development Bank also sees growth returning to 5.1 per cent in the 2026 financial year. But both institutions warn heavily: the projections rest on multiple ifs, including stable global demand, an improved investment climate and effective inflation control. Fitch Solutions, however, is more sceptical. It expects inflation to average 8.5 per cent in the 2025–26 financial year and believes that GDP growth will stay below the more optimistic projections, particularly if political uncertainty lingers. What holds back SEVERAL structural and external factors now combine to restrain Bangladesh. Investment slump: Both public capital expenditure and private investment have cooled as borrowing costs climb and investor confidence has weakened. Regulatory unpredictability and supply chain disruptions compound the issue. Policy and political uncertainty: Frequent regulatory changes, social unrest and transitions in government erode confidence. When businesses are uncertain of taxation, licensing or trade policy, they delay or abandon expansion. Inflation’s spread: Beyond consumer prices, inflation in inputs such as fuel, raw materials and energy raises costs for manufacturers and exporters, squeezing margins and investment viability. Climate costs: Rising heat and extreme weather are no longer fringe issues. They impose real economic losses and threaten health, infrastructure and labour productivity. Adaptation and resilience are becoming essential rather than optional. Financial sector weaknesses: Non-performing loans, declining capital adequacy, pressure on external reserves and weak regulatory oversight all pose risks to stability. The Aggregate Financial Stability Index shows these sectors dragging down overall resilience. Hope and policy moves DESPITE the headwinds, Bangladesh is taking steps that could help make the difference. It is tapping international support and will receive $1.33 billion from the International Monetary Fund under a combination of credit facilities and sustainability and resilience programmes, following successful reviews. This boosts external financing and supports macroeconomic stability. There is a growing push for monetary restraint and fiscal consolidation, including tighter control of subsidies, careful public expenditure and stronger revenue collection. These steps are essential to cool inflation and reduce deficit stress. Trade and export sectors remain resilient. Remittance inflows continue to provide a stabilising cushion to foreign exchange reserves, helping to repair external balances. Experts suggest renewed opportunity in diversification: increasing value addition in garments, expanding digital and technological services, improving agricultural productivity and investing in climate-resilient infrastructure. If properly managed, these could help unlock faster, more inclusive growth. What’s to be done TO RETAKE its earlier growth trajectory, Bangladesh needs to move beyond incremental fixes. Key priorities include tightening inflation control via supply-chain efficiency; improving market transparency and reducing rent-seeking in wholesale markets; strengthening local agricultural supply chains to reduce import dependency; and stabilising exchange rates with predictable monetary policy. Private investment stimulation requires simplifying regulations, ensuring consistency and enforcing property and contract law reliably; providing incentives for sectors with high potential, including value-added exports, technology and green energy; and improving access to finance with credit lines and risk mitigants. Financial sector stability demands cleaning up bad debt and ensuring banks maintain adequate capital; increasing oversight and transparency of financial institutions; and bolstering foreign reserve buffers to protect against external shocks. Climate resilience and adaptation call for investing in cooling infrastructure, urban greening and public health systems; increasing disaster preparedness, flood control and early warning systems; and mobilising international climate finance while integrating environmental risks into planning. Investment in human capital and inclusion means expanding vocational education, digital literacy and female labour participation; strengthening healthcare, especially in heat-exposed, rural and marginalised segments of the population; and focusing on equitable growth so that poorer households are not left behind. Governance and policy consistency and stability require reducing unpredictability; ensuring that business, taxation and trade rules are consistent; enhancing institutional capacity for evidence-based policy-making and regulatory enforcement; and strengthening the rule of law, contract enforcement and anti-corruption measures. If reforms are delayed or half-hearted, the cost will be steep. Inflation could entrench itself, eroding living standards; private investment may stay suppressed; labour unrest may rise; climate losses will accumulate; and social inequality may deepen. Bangladesh risks moving from a model of transition to one of stagnation. Bangladesh stands at a tipping point. The path it takes now — bold policy decisions, investment in resilience, clarity and inclusion — will determine whether it can revive its miracle and transform it into sustainable success. The world may have dimmed its spotlight slightly, but Bangladesh still has the raw materials, human capital, market size and export experience to secure a brighter chapter. It depends on treating this moment with urgency, coherence and vision. The miracle might yet be reborn, but only if it is reimagined. Professor Dr Zahurul Alam is the business faculty dean in the Canadian University of Bangladesh.

title: Communicating with aspiring migrants
body: ANNUALLY, more than a million Bangladeshis go abroad for work and remit foreign currency that has been propping up the economy for the past three decades, redirecting it from a foreign aid-based economy to a national resource-based one. But it is regrettable that they do not get preliminary information about migration and work overseas when they need it most. As a result, they get entrapped by various local touts, clandestinely engaged by different recruiting agencies, that feed aspiring migrants with false and fabricated information and allurements, based on which they take faulty decisions. This does not only ruin the aspirations of migrants to change their fortune but also eats into the core of whatever assets they have: scanty cash, land, households and, even, loans from banks and relatives. Against this backdrop, migration management needs to develop an effective communication strategy. Countries faring well with migration management, like the Philippines, Vietnam and Sri Lanka, have diligently improved their communication channels, tapping into empirical experiences and feedback from their migrant workers. The EU-based International Centre for Migration Policy Development has advocated developing a robust communication strategy for sending countries across the world.
