Energy builds quietly over decades and centuries, and when it is finally released, it does so through regional fault lines with devastating effect. The Dauki Fault, which hugs the southern edge of the Shillong Plateau and stretches roughly 300 kilometres, has long been recognised as a major seismic threat. The Madhupur Fault — about half that length but critically close to Dhaka — cuts through the heart of the country. These are not ancient scars of a bygone era. They remain active systems, identified in geological studies as among the most dangerous in South Asia, with the potential to generate earthquakes in the range of magnitude 7.0 to 8.5. History confirms the risk. The region has endured destructive earthquakes over the centuries, many linked to the same tectonic stresses that persist today. In Bangladesh, no region can accurately be described as ‘safe’, only varying degrees of vulnerable. And with the population now denser and cities more sprawling than ever before, the consequences of a major rupture would be far worse than in the past. Recent tremors — modest in strength but frequent enough to unsettle — have brought the Madhupur Fault back into national conversation. Experts have warned repeatedly that this fault could produce a major earthquake ‘at any time’. Its proximity to heavily populated centres such as Dhaka, Gazipur, Tangail and Mymensingh magnifies the threat. Government assessments suggest that even a magnitude-6.9 event along this fault could render hundreds of thousands of buildings in Dhaka unsafe or destroyed. The Dauki Fault, meanwhile, remains the region’s unpredictable force. Its last major rupture occurred centuries ago, and several studies estimate its return interval at between 350 and 650 years — a timeframe that many scientists believe places us uncomfortably close to its next release of pressure. What intensifies the danger is not merely the expected magnitude of such quakes but the very ground upon which Bangladesh is built. Much of the country rests on young alluvial soil — soft sediment laid down by rivers over millennia — which tends to amplify seismic waves. Dhaka is particularly exposed: countless buildings sit atop reclaimed wetlands, many lack proper engineering standards, and building codes are frequently ignored in the rush to expand. The potential outcome is disturbing. RAJUK’s own studies warn that a single moderate-to-strong earthquake on the Madhupur Fault could collapse or severely damage over 860,000 structures in the capital, cause immense loss of life and inflict economic harm in the tens of billions. Such projections may read like the backdrop to a dystopian novel, but they remain grounded in sober scientific analysis. Despite years of caution from researchers, preparedness remains worryingly limited. Regulations exist but are poorly enforced. Older buildings remain unassessed and unretrofitted. Urban growth continues to play out with little regard for seismic risk. Public awareness of what to do during and after a quake remains minimal and drills are rare. The scale of the danger requires a response that is serious, coordinated and sustained. This means enforcing building codes without exception, investing in the retrofitting of vulnerable structures, expanding geological mapping of fault lines, and making earthquake education a routine part of civic life. It also means developing emergency response systems that reflect the realities of dense urban living. The truth is unavoidable: the ground beneath Bangladesh is not passive. It moves, strains and releases energy on its own timetable, indifferent to human schedules or unpreparedness. The Dauki and Madhupur faults are not abstract features on a map; they represent potential flashpoints for national catastrophe. The tremors we have felt in recent years are reminders — gentle ones, for now — of what might come. The longer the country delays serious action, the narrower the margin becomes between warning and disaster. Dr Makhan Lal Dutta, an irrigation engineer, is chairman and CEO of Harvesting Knowledge Consultancy.

title: Soil management and food security
body: Soil, the foundation of life, is a living entity and a basic component of the environment. Still, 95 per cent of our food comes from soils. It is home to nearly 59 per cent of Earth’s species, and there are more living organisms in a tablespoon of healthy soil than people on Earth. Various micro- and macro-organisms (eg, fungi, bacteria, and over 2,700 species of earthworms) are vital yet under-appreciated creatures that keep our soil alive and fertile. Soils supply 15 of the 18 naturally occurring chemical elements essential to plants. Over 2 billion people worldwide suffer from a lack of micronutrients, known as hidden hunger. Healthy food, a healthy climate and a healthy planet are all impossible without healthy soil. Beyond food, soil is a mighty ally in mitigating and adapting to climate change. Globally, 33 per cent of soils are degraded. It can take up to 1,000 years to produce just 2–3 centimetres of soil but only moments to destroy it. Against this background, the International Union of Soil Sciences, in 2002, adopted a resolution proposing that December 5 be marked as World Soil Day to highlight the importance of soil as a critical component of the natural system and as a vital contributor to human well-being. The date was chosen because it corresponds with the official birthday of the late Bhumibol Adulyadej, King of Thailand, who was one of the main proponents of this initiative. Later, the FAO Conference, in June 2013, unanimously endorsed World Soil Day and requested its official adoption at the 68th session of the UN General Assembly. In December 2013, UNGA 68 declared December 5 as World Soil Day. It became an official international day in 2014, and since then the Day has been held annually to focus attention on the importance of healthy soil and to advocate for the sustainable management of soil resources. The Day raises awareness of the relationship between humans and soil and of their role in soil management in ensuring soil biodiversity and improving soil health, reducing erosion and pollution, enhancing water filtration and storage, achieving sustainable and resilient agrifood systems, and contributing to carbon sequestration. The celebration is also important for raising awareness among policymakers and the general public about possible solutions to national and local soil degradation. This year’s theme is ‘Healthy Soils for Healthy Cities’. Soil is where our food begins: no soil, no food, no life, no civilisation. The first civilisations of humankind were built on irrigated agriculture primarily because irrigated lands remained productive much longer. The fertile soils and reliable water supply enabled farmers to produce a large surplus of food and ensured continuity in the food supply. Most historians agree that the first civilisations developed in three regions — the Nile Valley, Mesopotamia, and the Indus Valley — owing to (1) fertile soils, (2) dependable irrigation, and (3) resistance to soil erosion. The stability of the land made it possible for farmers to cultivate the same land for many generations. This allowed people to settle and build permanent homes. Permanent settlement during the Neolithic era (~12,000 years ago, Global Land Outlook) led to recurrent exploitation or overexploitation of the same land and soil, resulting in degradation. A growing population, together with increasing and diversified demand for ecosystem goods and services, has put tremendous pressure on natural resources. With the progress of civilisation, humans have learned many skills, but rarely have they learned to preserve their source of food. Civilised humans have despoiled most of the lands on which they have lived, and this has been a major cause of the decline of civilisations in older settled regions. A Chinese proverb states: ‘If cities are destroyed and farms remain intact, cities will grow spontaneously, but if farms are destroyed, then cities will perish automatically.’ When farms, forests, and grasslands fail to produce a surplus, cities wither and die. The fundamental cause of the decline of civilisations in most regions was the deterioration of the natural resource base on which those civilisations rested, with frequently cited causes of degradation including overpopulation, war, colonisation, climate change, moral decay, political corruption, economic maladjustment, and poor leadership. Modern technology and enterprise have made it possible for us to develop and exploit natural resources faster than any people in history. The great majority have exploited these resources without regard for the future. It is not necessary to destroy natural resources in order to use them. We can conserve most resources while still maximising benefits. Global natural resources are limited, and we must be conservative in using them to achieve the land degradation neutrality target by 2030 set by the UNGA and the UNCCD. We must not allow further degradation of the planet’s resources before unlocking their full potential for human well-being. With improving technology and genuine conservation, the world’s land resources can continue to support us in the years to come. All renewable resources — soils, forests, grasslands, water, and wildlife — will produce more under well-managed conservation programmes than if wantonly exploited. Up to 58 per cent more food could be produced through sustainable soil management (FAO). In Bangladesh, more than half of the population suffers from malnutrition. Severe acute malnutrition affects 450,000 children, while close to two million children suffer moderate acute malnutrition. Nutrient deficiencies stem from the wide consumption of nutrient-poor staple crops grown on nutrient-depleted soils. The intensification of agriculture with several harvests per year of HYV crops and heavy chemical inputs has led to declining soil fertility and jeopardised food security (FAO). Average cropping intensity is 198 per cent. Nationally, land degradation (moderate to very severe) accounts for 11.24 million hectares or 76.2 per cent in 2020, with annual degradation of around 27,000 hectares during 2000–2020. Deficiency of nitrogen is widespread in Bangladesh’s soils. In addition, severe or very severe depletion of P (5.88 Mha), K (3.33 Mha), S (5.27 Mha), Zn (5.16 Mha), and B (3.83 Mha) has been reported. Degraded land with respect to soil nutrient depletion is estimated at around 11.07 million hectares (75 per cent of the country). Regionally, Mymensingh, Chattogram, and Rangpur divisions are more degraded in terms of soil fertility. Soil organic matter (SOM) is regarded as the lifeline of soil. Good agricultural soils contain 3–6 per cent SOM. In Bangladesh, there is widespread depletion of soil organic matter (78.7 per cent of the country area). Excessive dependence on chemical inputs due to soil fertility depletion may eventually lead to soil toxicity. Depletion of soil fertility is at the root of land degradation and desertification, intensifying climate vulnerability. There remains a particular dearth of information on the impacts of climate change on land and on the economics of temperature rise, especially localised temperature increases. Agrarian Bangladesh has limited land resources. Net cropped area was 8.08 million hectares in 2000–2001, 7.929 million hectares in 2011–2012, 8.126 million hectares in 2019–2020 (this increase may be due to the inclusion of char lands, i.e., at the cost of water resource depletion), and then decreased to 8.028 million hectares in 2022–2023 (BBS 2001, 2012, 2020, 2024). Per capita cropped area (~0.044 ha) is decreasing because of a booming population (MoEF 2007), meaning per capita food-producing land is shrinking. Bangladesh is also losing around 69,000 hectares of arable land (SRDI, 2013), mostly to unplanned urbanisation and infrastructure development leading to soil sealing. Population growth, decreasing NCA, and adverse climate are exerting a triangular pressure on remaining land. Meeting the food demand of an ever-increasing population from dwindling land resources is a Herculean task. Our soil is sick (degraded) due to greedy overexploitation and malnutrition, and needs proper care. The Global Soil Doctor programme may be implemented countrywide to improve farmers’ technical knowledge on soil health, food security, and human nutrition (FAO). Diversifying cropping systems, crop rotation (shallow-rooted crops followed by deep-rooted ones to avoid nutrient leaching, low nutrient-demanding crops followed by high nutrient-demanding ones including nitrogen-fixing or legume crops) instead of mono-cropping, climate-smart agriculture, no-tillage farming to reduce soil erosion, mulching and crop sanitation, and replacing chemical fertilisers and pesticides with organic alternatives — along with the application of SLM and IPM technologies — are some solutions that can lead to healthier soils, increased biodiversity, and more nutritious foods. The National Environment Policy 2018 places due importance on optimising population size to attain a balance between people and resources and avoid land degradation. The National Land Use Policy 2001 needs urgent upgrading to address current challenges. We must reorient our outlook from maximising production and revenue to restoring soil health. In Bangladesh, urbanisation is increasing, and farmers will not be able to produce enough safe food for themselves or for city dwellers unless conservation efforts begin now. To build healthier cities, we must urgently change our current consumption patterns of natural resources and the way we feed people. We must safeguard our resource base by avoiding and reducing land degradation and restoring degraded land. History shows that the fall of civilisations around the world was fundamentally linked to land degradation, and dependence on other nations for food is not a viable option. Though late, a fully rounded programme of soil conservation is essential for continued peace and prosperity. So, this World Soil Day and every day, let us celebrate our soil, nourish it and protect it. Dr Md Sohrab Ali is a former additional director general, Department of Environment.

title: City lives if soil lives
body: WORLD Soil Day today reminds us that soil is not merely agricultural land, it is the essential foundation of life, urban environment and social stability. Since 2014, the day has been observed in honour of King Bhumibol Adulyadej of Thailand, whose initiatives demonstrated that sustainable development begins with healthy soil. The theme for 2025 is ‘Healthy Soil, Healthy City.’ Urban soil is the invisible foundation of daily lives. It supports food production, maintains ecological balance, regulates water, sustains biodiversity and plays a crucial role in human well-being. Yet, rapid urbanisation, high-rise construction, infrastructure expansion and the dominance of concrete have pushed urban soils into neglect. As a result, the city’s ecosystems are weakening, food security is threatened and climate resilience is diminishing. Beneath every brick and stone of the city lies soil, the core of urban life. Soil health in cities refers not only to fertility but to the soil’s overall ability to sustain ecosystems, maintain productivity, protect the environment and support human physical and mental well-being. Healthy urban soil is the foundation of environmental resilience. It absorbs excess water, mitigates flooding, captures and stores atmospheric carbon, reduces pollution and keeps green and open spaces vibrant. Healthy soil is built on seven essential qualities: adequate nutrients, stable structure, root-friendly depth, good drainage, rich microbial life, non-toxicity and resilience against stress. When any of this declines, the soil begins to lose its vitality. Urbanisation is increasing worldwide. According to a 2019 United Nations report, more than half of the global population now lives in urban areas. By 2050, the world population will exceed nine billion, with a significant portion living in cities. Rapid urban expansion may cause the loss of nearly 2 per cent of farm land. In countries such as Bangladesh, unplanned urban development is shrinking water bodies, green spaces and open lands, putting intense pressure on urban soils. Dhaka offers a clear example. Before independence, in 1961, the city’s population was 2.6 million, with only about 5 per cent living in urban areas. According to the 2022 census, the urban population has reached 53.7 million, about 32 per cent of the total population. Most of the city is now covered by concrete, disrupting natural water systems, increasing flood risk, raising temperatures and degrading ecological services. As humans move farther away from soil, long-term health risks rise, which is a reality now well-established scientifically. A recent the World Economic Forum report notes that beneficial microbes found in soil closely resemble those in the human gut, influencing immunity and mental stability. With reduced soil contact in urban life, the risk of autoimmune disorders may rise. Research also shows that soil bacteria such as Mycobacterium vaccae help to reduce depression and strengthen the immune system. Gardening or even brief contact with green spaces reduces stress and enhances overall wellness. Urban agriculture depends heavily on healthy soil. Properly managed urban farming not only produces nutritious food but also strengthens social cohesion through community gardens and resilient local networks. Healthy soil acts as a natural filter, purifying and storing water, preventing pollution, supporting plant growth and protecting human health. Yet, the soil beneath our cities is losing life rapidly. In Dhaka, more than 80 per cent of the land is covered by concrete. This disrupts water infiltration, causes severe water stagnation even after light rain, reduces green spaces, raises temperatures and lowers productivity. Such an unplanned urban growth weakens the soil’s ability to sequester carbon, provide ecological services and regulate the urban climate. Contaminated soils increase health risks while urban expansion destroys fertile land. Although discussions on urban soil health have increased in recent years, research remains limited and largely focused on pollution and risk factors. But the social, environmental and nutritional benefits of urban farming are equally important. During the International Year of Soils, Bristol’s Urban Soil Declaration’ showed that citizens can bring soil health into mainstream conversation. Today, sustainable urban thinking around the world highlights cities not as consumption hubs but as regenerative spaces through composting, green linkage and soil restoration. Thus, improving urban soil is not only a scientific undertaking but also foundational to building healthier and more humane cities. To keep urban soil healthy, consistent small steps are essential: creating diverse green spaces, promoting rooftop and community gardens, converting organic waste into compost, reducing plastic and encouraging walking, cycling and public transport. These actions reduce pressure on soil, strengthen its structure and support biodiversity. Awareness is equally vital. Neighbours, local authorities and policymakers must recognise that surface greenery protects the underground web of life. Planting trees in flood-prone zones enhances water retention, stabilises soil and reduces erosion. Avoiding contaminated soil and maintaining hygiene are crucial as well. Policy-level actions such as protecting water bodies, ensuring soil reuse after excavation, conserving agricultural land, training farmers and encouraging soil-focused research among planners are now urgent. A healthy city is not defined by skyscrapers but by the vitality of the soil beneath them. When urban soil is healthy, city life becomes sustainable, healthy and humane. Prioritising soil in policies, planning and civic initiatives will ensure environmental, social and economic stability. The future of cities stands on the strength of their soils. Protecting and restoring soil are now the most essential step towards securing the future of urban life. Dr Md Saiful Islam Bhuiyan ([email protected]) is a professor of soil science in Sher-e-Bangla Agricultural University

title: India’s border action undermines law, trust
body: INDIA’S continued push-in along the Bangladesh border marks a troubling departure from diplomatic norms, legal obligations and the principles of neighbourly conduct. The latest incident, in which 30 people were forcibly pushed through the Tentulbaria border in Meherpur, shows that this is no longer a matter of sporadic lapses but a sustained pattern. Since May 7, at least 2,402 people have been pushed into Bangladesh. There are Rohingya refugees and even Indians among them. The Indian authorities have pushed at least 223 Rohingyas across the border, including 50 registered with the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees in India. Their accounts follow the same troubling sequence: detention by the Indian police, confinement in various facilities and then expulsion without due legal process. The Calcutta High Court has already declared such deportation unlawful and instructed that Indians pushed into Bangladesh should be brought back, lending weight to Dhaka’s long-held position that India’s border practices increasingly breach the international law and bilateral agreements. Bangladesh has consistently stated, through official channels, that it remains ready to take back any Bangladeshis residing illegally in India as long as the repatriation takes place through recognised, formal procedures. New Delhi, however, has yet to respond in any meaningful way and this silence has effectively allowed the practice to continue, further straining a relationship already under considerable pressure and unsettling the communities that live along the frontiers. Alongside the push-ins, the continuing killing of Bangladeshis along the border remains just as alarming, a grim reality that India has failed to resolve despite repeated assurances. More than 30 Bangladeshis wer killed in 2025 alone. Recent cases, including the shooting of a young farmer in Lalmonirhat and the deaths of two men in Chapainawabganj, have reinforced the perception that India’s professed ‘no lethal weapon policy’ exists more on paper than in practice. For border communities, everyday tasks such as tending fields, caring for livestock or moving through shared spaces have become fraught with danger. Matters have worsened with reports of Indian forces attempting to construct fencing near the zero line, in a clear contravention of bilateral agreements on the placement of border infrastructure. These developments, taken together with the push-ins, erode trust, undermine prospects for cooperative border management and expose the widening gulf between India’s official commitments and its actions on the ground. Bangladesh cannot allow such violations of sovereignty, humanitarian standards and diplomatic commitments to be normalised. Dhaka must, therefore, raise the issue at relevant United Nations platforms, regional bodies and international human rights forums to ensure that such persistent violations should receive the scrutiny that they demand. New Delhi needs to realise that true neighbourliness requires respect, restraint and adherence to the rule of law. It is now up to India to demonstrate these values not merely in declaration, but in practice.

title: Unapproved soya bean oil price increase grossly undermining
body: AN UNAPPROVED increase in the price of soya bean oil, selling for Tk 197 a litre, up by Tk 9, on the market on December 2, is gravely worrying in that it undermines government authority, harms consumer rights and creates a form of impunity that encourages further such increases in future. The trade body of oil refiners and manufacturers has increased the soya bean oil price, with a five-litre bottle selling for Tk 956 against the earlier price of Tk 922. The commerce adviser to the interim government on December 3 said that the traders had increased the price without ministerial approval, noting that the ministry would take action in this regard. But traders claim that they increased the price in accordance with due procedure, which includes seeking ministerial approval in a letter sent on November 10. The traders say that they had waited for a reply and the ministry did not reply in 15 days. They then increased the price assuming that the government would have responded if the proposal for the price increase had been illogical. The assumption by the traders on the price increase is grossly undermining. The Bangladesh Vegetable Oil Refiners and Vanaspati Manufacturers’ Association on October 13 also tried to increase prices of edible oils by Tk 5–6 a litre by issuing a press release, noting that it was an alignment with prices on the international market. The commerce ministry denied giving any approval, noting that it had not made a final decision on the price increase. The commerce adviser on December 3 also said that the government had bought five million litres of soya bean oil through a tender process in which the traders offered a price Tk 20 below the market price, nullifying the traders’ grounds for seeking an increase in price. The government on September 22 increased the price of edible oils by Tk 1 a litre against the refiners’ demand for a Tk 10 increase. The government also increased the price of edible oil on April 22 by up to Tk 14 a litre. Soya bean oil prices also went up by Tk 5 a litre in the middle of January. In the case of the October attempts by traders to increase prices, the government sounded a warning, but it did not take any action. The latest incident appears to have happened riding on the indolence of the government at that time. Traders keep arm-twisting the government now, as they did during the Awami League government that fell on August 5, 2024. It is time that the government acts stringently. Such moves by the traders would, otherwise, keep undermining government authority, harming consumer interests and creating a form of impunity.

title: NATO’s 5 per cent gamble
body: THE agreement by NATO members to raise defence spending to 5 per cent of gross domestic product by 2035 has been welcomed across western capitals as a moment of strategic clarity. After years of uneven commitments and familiar hand-wringing, the alliance finally appears ready to shoulder more responsibility in a world that feels less secure by the day. The decision may strengthen deterrence in the short term, yet it also contains the seeds of a structural imbalance that could reshape transatlantic relations in ways Europeans have not fully reckoned with. At first glance, a pledge to spend more on defence looks like an overdue response to Russian aggression, an acknowledgment that Europe must rebuild its own capabilities and reduce its dependence on Washington. The political symbolism is powerful. Leaders who once hesitated to discuss even 2 per cent of gross domestic product now support dramatic increases. The narrative of European awakening is enticing. Yet it draws attention away from a deeper question: who actually gains from this sudden surge of spending. Europe has the political will to spend more, but it does not have the industrial capacity to match its ambitions. Years of neglect hollowed out domestic weapons manufacturing and investment stalled in key areas of research, development, and production. The result is a continent that may be prepared to buy more weapons, but not one that can easily build them at scale. That reality points to an uncomfortable conclusion. A significant share of Europe’s new defence budgets will flow not to European producers but to American defence manufacturers that remain dominant in advanced systems, logistics, and technology. This is not a conspiracy or a hidden scheme. It is a structural outcome. The United States built a vast military industrial base over decades, while Europe often preferred to rely on the umbrella of American security guarantees. Now that threat perceptions have changed, Europe is trying to strengthen its defence posture, but it has little choice but to turn to American suppliers for the most critical equipment. The more Europe spends, the more embedded it becomes in US defence ecosystems. Instead of achieving greater independence, it risks deeper dependence. This shift offers Washington several strategic advantages. First, it strengthens the American defence industry at a moment when global competition is intensifying. Second, it reinforces US leverage within NATO. A Europe that relies heavily on American technology, training, and logistics remains firmly anchored in a US-led security structure. Third, it enhances Washington’s bargaining power in its dealings with Russia. A stronger NATO is often interpreted as a warning to Moscow, but it also equips the United States with more diplomatic tools. Washington can present itself as the indispensable leader of a revitalized alliance, something it may choose to wield in negotiations or crises. For Europe, the implications are mixed. On one hand, increased defence spending does improve readiness and resilience. On the other, it raises the risk of long-term misalignment between political aspirations and practical outcomes. European leaders speak frequently about strategic autonomy, but autonomy requires more than large budgets. It requires coherent planning, shared priorities, and industrial cooperation. Without these, the 5 percent commitment becomes a fiscal gesture rather than a strategic transformation. There are also domestic consequences that European leaders will soon confront. Voters across the continent already face rising living costs, strained public services, and growing political polarization. Redirecting vast sums toward defence will inevitably shape future elections. In societies where political trust is fragile, the public may question why so much money is being spent on weapons rather than schools, hospitals, or climate resilience. If public support falters, governments may struggle to sustain the very spending they have promised. The greatest risk is that the 5 per cent target becomes a symbol that masks underlying weaknesses. Europe might appear stronger on paper, but without robust industrial foundations and a clear strategic vision, higher spending will not necessarily translate into meaningful capability. The alliance could slip into a cycle where announcements of funding increases substitute for long-term planning. That would leave NATO with impressive numbers but uneven readiness. It is worth noting that NATO plans a review in 2029 to assess the trajectory and ensure the spending path remains realistic and credible. Not all members are on equal footing: countries like Spain have opted out of the 5 per cent pledge, reflecting different political priorities and fiscal capacities across Europe. Analysts from the International Institute for Strategic Studies caution that many European nations still lack the industrial base to scale up advanced capabilities rapidly, reinforcing the argument that higher spending may disproportionately benefit US defence contractors. Moreover, the 5 per cent includes security-related spending such as assistance to Ukraine as well as cyber, infrastructure, and resilience programs, not solely hardware procurement, which nuances the idea that Europe will automatically spend more on weapons. None of this means Europe should ignore emerging threats or shy away from investing in its own defence. The challenge is to ensure that higher spending aligns with genuine capacity-building rather than reinforcing structural dependency. That requires cooperation among European states, investment in shared production, and the discipline to prioritize strategic needs over political symbolism. It also requires a candid conversation about what kind of partnership Europe wants with the United States. A healthier transatlantic relationship will come not from Europe spending more for the sake of appearances, but from Europe building credible capabilities of its own. The 5 per cent pledge has been hailed as a historic breakthrough, yet its deeper meaning is far more complex. It may bolster deterrence in the near term, but it also reflects a Europe that is still searching for its strategic identity. Unless European leaders address the underlying imbalances within NATO, the new spending commitments could lock the continent into a future where its security is expensive, yet not truly its own. CounterPunch.org, December 3. Imran Khalid is a geostrategic analyst and columnist on international affairs.

title: Romel Rahman wins Pratidhwani Story Prize
body: Writer Romel Rahman has won the 1st Pratidhwani Story Prize 2025, said a release. The online literary magazine Pratidhwani organised the competition, Natun Galper Sandhane, which received more than 300 submissions. Romel won the prize, announced on December 26, for his story ‘Kurchiana.’ Pratidhwani editor Shakhawat Tipu said that the Kurchiana had won the prise for unique storytelling. Romel will receive $100 in prize money. Pratidhwani will publish a collection of 10 best stories, the release said.

title: Bangla Academy hands over awards, fellowships
body: The 48th annual general meeting of the Bangla Academy was held on Saturday with various programmes, including a fellowship and an award ceremony. The annual general meeting, attended by the academy members, fellows and guests, began with the national anthem and a recitation of religious scriptures. Bangla Academy director general Mohammad Azam, in his yearly report, said that the academy aims to work more on research across the country. The academy president professor Abul Kasem Fazlul Haque, who chaired the event, said that the academy has worked for 70 years and tries to fulfil people’s expectations despite many limitations. The Bangla Academy handed over its honorary fellowships to seven personalities for their outstanding contributions to their respective fields. The recipients of the honorary fellowships are Philip Gaine in Journalism category, professor Mahbub Ullah in economics, painter Samar Majumdar and architect Marina Tabassum in fine arts, professor Parveen Hasan in history and professor Bijon Kumar Shil in science category. The fellows received medals, certificates and floral crests at the event. Besides, the academy handed over eight awards for 2025 for their contributions to literature, research, science, theatre and translation. Professor Mansur Musa received the Mohammad Barkatullah Essay Literature Award 2025 while Khosru Chowdhury received the Meher Kabir Science Literature Award 2025 and Poet Sanaul Haque Khan received the Mazharul Islam Poetry Award 2025. Hafiz Rashid Khan received the Sadat Ali Akhand Literature Award 2025 while renowned theatre activist Tariq Anam Khan received professor Momtazuddin Ahmed Theatre Award 2025 and Shibbrata Barman received Abu Rushd Literature Award 2025. Halima-Sharafuddin Science Award 2025 was received by Safiq Islam, and Subrata Barua received Rabeya Khatun Fiction Award 2025 at the event.

title: Spardha premiered four plays
body: Spardha Academy of Performing Arts premiered four short duration stage play as a part of their extensive six- module direction course at Spardha Atelier in Gulshan 2 in the capital on Friday and Saturday. The direction course was conducted under the supervision of renowned theatre scholar and director Syed Jamil Ahmed featuring four directors namely Ahmed Opu, Aniruddha Anu, Fariha Jannat Mim, and Shanaj Parvin Jonaki, said a press release. On Friday, the academy premiered Precisely, directed by Ahmed Opu and written by Harold Pinter and Camera Doesn’t Love Anyone, directed by Fariha Jannat Mim and written by Dalia Taha. Palestinian poet and playwright Dalia Taha’s The Camera Doesn’t Love Anyone, shows two women tell a story about the way a third woman tells the story of her murdered husband. They narrate their experiences which make them traumatised, and while they are forced to talk, the journalist does not believe their statements. Shorme Akter, Marshia Shawon and Tomal Moulik played the characters. Harold Pinter’s Precisely shows two civil servants discussing the hecatombs of death that would follow a nuclear attack and arrogantly determine the exact numbers to be expected. Majbaul Hasan Arnob, Sanjida Yasmin Snigdha, Kumar Uday, Tareq Shuvo and Rumman Shahriar Shuvo played the characters here. On Saturday, Words, Words, Words was staged, directed by Aniruddha Anu and written by David Ives. Then Applicant was staged, which was directed by Shanaj Parvin Jonaki and written by Harold Pinter. Theatre troupe Spardha: Independent Theatre Collective, brings popular theatre productions including 4.48 Montrash, Ami Birangana Bolchhi and Jibon o Rajnoitik Bastobota and they regularly organise workshops with the aim to produce skilled theatre activists since 2018.

title: James’s concert in Faridpur postponed due to clash
body: A concert by rock singer Faruq Mahfuz Anam James, who is also known as Nagar Baul, was cancelled on Friday night following clashes on the Faridpur Zilla School campus in Faridpur district during the institution’s 185th anniversary celebrations. The clashes left at least three people injured. The concert was scheduled to begin at about 9:30pm on the school premises as the closing event of the two-day reunion programme. Chinmoy Kar, one of the organisers, said that the concert was postponed due to the clashes between school alumni and local people who wanted to enter the school campus to enjoy the concert. ‘The school campus was filled with alumni and current students but local people tried to enter the ground, which resulted in the clashes. At about 10.00pm, we cancelled the concert following instructions from the Faridpur deputy commissioner,’ said Chinmoy, adding that they would organise the concert at a suitable time. Faridpur superintendent of police Md Nazrul Islam said that no case was file in this connection. ‘Some outsiders tried to enter the campus to enjoy James’ performance and created the chaos,’ he said.

title: Digital reality poses threat to intellectual practice: discussion
body: Participants at a discussion said on Friday that the digital reality created a new threat for human labour and intellectual practices that would have impacts on the civilisation. They also said that literature creates a relationship between human and memory, while literature magazines help to create community. They made the remarks at a discussion titled Bangladesher Sahitya Patrikar Sanskriti, organised by study-circle based online literature magazine Oaakakha, their first printed issue launch event at Bangla Academy in the capital. Oaakakha, the quarterly literature magazine comprises articles, short-stories, poems, book reviews, interviews, features and reports on their print version which was jointly edited by Sagar Mallick and Tanjum Shakib. Poet and thinker Farhad Mazhar, fiction writer and National Book Centre director Afsana Begum, and Bangla Academy director general Mohammad Azam spoke at the event. Afsana Begum said that Oaakakha works a lot in study circles and their online discussion also attracted a lot of audiences which is inspiring for cultural practices. ‘Their first issue of the magazine is well designed and rich in contents. The process of bringing out a magazine helps a lot to collect experiences for organisers, the failure of any publications cannot indicate that the initiative itself is a failure,’ Afsana Begum said, adding that digital reality decreased the number of publications. Mohammad Azam said that the lack of quality writings is the main crisis for magazines. ‘80s little magazine movement made literature magazines in Bangladesh popular, and successful magazines need many elements including contemporary literature, issues, trends and its acceptance as a product,’ Mohammad Azam said, adding that the online reality creates new threats on creative publications but online and print versions can run simultaneously. Farhad Mazhar said that the concept of literature is not clear in the society and it is translated as entertainment which has created a crisis in communication. ‘The learner of books and oral narrative are totally different, while digital technology based information creates instant reaction without rationality, memory and myth of the people,’ he said, adding that literature creates a relationship between human and collective memory. Farhad Mazhar also warned that the latest digital technology, which was created as an alternative to human labour, has decreased importance of human presence at working places, war field and entertainment, which will also result in decreased remittance earning from developed countries. The event also had an open discussion and musical event performed by Humayun Azam Rewaz.

title: Syed Shamsul Haq’s birth anniv today
body: Today is the 90th anniversary of birth of poet-playwright and fiction writer Syed Shamsul Haq. Born in Kurigram on December 27, 1935, Syed Shamsul Haq started writing at an early age. He enrolled at Dhaka University’s English department but did not complete the degree. His first story titled Udayasta was published in Fazle Lohani-edited literary magazine ‘Agatya’ in 1951. He penned several collections of poems such as ‘Ekada Ek Rajye’, ‘Biratihin Utsab’, ‘Baishakhe Rachita Pangktimala’, ‘Nabhimule Bhasmadhar’, ‘Pratidhwanigan’, ‘Ami Janmagrahan Karini’, ‘Paraner Gahin Bhitar’ and ‘Apar Purush’. He also earned acclaim for writing fictions, including ‘Jaleshwarir Galpagulo’, ‘Prachin Bangsher Nihswa Santan’, ‘Nishiddha Loban’, ‘Khelaram Khele Ja’, ‘Stabdhatar Anubad’, ‘Raktagolap’, ‘Tumi Sei Tarbari’, ‘Anander Mrityu’ and ‘Neel Dangshan’. He created a new trend in contemporary Bangla drama with his plays in verse such as ‘Payer Awaj Paoya Jay’, ‘Nuruldiner Sara Jiban’, ‘Ekhane Ekhan’, ‘Irsha’, ‘Narigan’, and ‘Banglar Mati Banglar Jal’. For his contribution to Bangla literature, he received the Bangla Academy Award, Ekushey Padak and Independence Award. Syed Shamsul Haq passed away on September 27, 2016.

title: Rabeya Khatun’s birth anniv today
body: Today is the 90th anniversary of birth of Independence Award-winning novelist Rabeya Khatun. Rabeya Khatun was born in Munshiganj on December 27, 1935 to Maulavi Mohammad Mulluk Chand and Hamida Khatun. Her debut novel ‘Madhumati’ was published in 1963. The fiction writer made her mark in Bangla literature by writing novels such as ‘Saheb Bazar’, ‘Man Ek Shwetkapati’, ‘Pherari Surja’, ‘Anekjaner Ekjan’, ‘Jibaner Arek Naam’, ‘Dibash Rajani’, ‘Mohar Ali’, ‘Sei Ek Basante’, ‘Pakhi Sab Kare Rab’, ‘Neel Nishit’ and ‘Bayanna Galir Ek Gali’. A number of her works have been adapted into films, including Fazlul Haque-directed ‘President’, Chashi Nazrul Islam-directed ‘Dhrubatara’ and ‘Megher Pore Megh’, Moushumi-directed Kakhano Megh Kakhano Brishti, Shahjahan Chowdhurt-directed Madhumati and Taher Shipon-directed Ekattarer Nishan. Besides, her works also have been adapted into teleplays and drama series. For her contribution to Bangla literature, Rabeya Khatun received Ekushey Padak in 1993 and Independence Award in 2017. She also received numerous awards, including Bangla Academy Literary Award, Humayun Kadir Memorial Award, Lekhika Sangha Award, Nasiruddin Gold Medal, Sher-e-Bangla Gold Medal, Jasimuddin Award, Wrishiz Shahitya Padak and Michael Madhusudan Award. Rabeya Khatun passed away on January 3, 2021.

title: Bangladeshi expatriate community in Malaysia celebrates victory day
body: Bangladeshi students in Malaysia celebrated the 54th national victory day of Bangladesh at Mercure Kuala Lumpur Trion on Thursday, said a press release. The event titled Bijoy Sondha consisted of musical performance, poem recitations, mime performance and theatre performance, organised by Bangladeshi Expat Community in Malaysia. Rashna Sharmeen performed a poem recitation while a drama titled Paka Kotha was performed by Sumaiya Haque and Tarequal Islam Tareque at the event. Performed by Bilkis Mir, a mono drama titled Naiori, written, designed and directed by Ahmed Musa, was staged. Sumaiya Haque and Tarequal Islam Tareque also performed mime at the event. ‘Bangladeshi students and professionals also participated at the event which also promoted the history and culture of Bangladesh in Malaysia,’ said Tarequal Islam Tareque, one of the organisers of the community.

title: 4-day cultural festival under way at Bengal Shilpalay
body: To mark Bangladesh’s victory month, a four-day cultural festival titled Prane Ano Gaan is under way at the Bengal Shilpalay of Dhanmondi in the capital. The festival, comprising music, poetry recitation, visual art, crafts, and creative activities of children and young people, was inaugurated on Wednesday. On the second day, Bhaswar Bandyopadhyay recited from the poet Jasimuddin’s Nakshi Kanthar Math, while singer Bijan Chandra Mistri performed Bangla thumri, and Champa Banik rendered popular film songs of Bangladesh in the evening. Folk-singer Labik Kamal Gaurab also rendered diverse folk songs at the event. As part of the festival, the Quamrul Hassan Exhibition Hall is hosting a group of exhibition titled The Other Voice, featuring selected works by 35 women artists from the Bengal Foundation and Abul Khair Collections. A curated fair of selected rural handicrafts and artisanal products titled Karukatha was also held as a part of the event. Today, the event features songs based on three poets performed by Azizur Rahman Tuhin, modern Nazrul songs by Susmita Debnath Suchi, a literary reading by Raihanul Amin Kollol, and Rabindra Sangeet by Aditi Mohsin. On the closing day, December 27, the festival will wrap up with musical performances of Mahua Manjari Sunanda, Farzana Wahid Sayan and Tuntun Baul. The festival was formally inaugurated on Wednesday by Abdul Hai Sarker, Chairman of Dhaka Bank, in the presence of Abul Khair, Chairman of Bengal Foundation, and Luva Nahid Choudhury, Director General of Bengal Foundation.

title: 3-day Birju Maharaj Kathak dance festival ends in Dhaka
body: Three-day 14th Pandit Birju Maharaj Kathak Dance Festival 1432 ended at the auditorium of the Guide House at Baily Road in Dhaka on Thursday. The festival, organised by Kathak Nritya Shamproday, was inaugurated on December 23, with fifty dancers across the country participating. At the closing day of the event, dance troupes Nritya Ashram, Chanda Malika, Samarpan Kala Kendra, Rinijhini Lalitakala Academy Rangpur, Nataraj Nrittyakala Kendra Noakhali and Nikkon Academy Chattogram performed dance recital. Young dancers Tuli Mallik, Nirjhar Das Adi, Imama Ashmi and Arjasshi Bishwash Pritha, among others, performed on Thursday, while renowned dancers including Monira Parveen, Emon Kumar Dey, Deepa Sarkar and Fifa Chakma gave dance recitals. A commemorative discussion on eminent dancer and teacher, ‘Nritya Mata Guru: Rahija Khanam Jhunu’ was also held on the closing day of the festival. On the opening day Kathak Nritya Shamproday staged a dance drama titled ‘Prasanga 47’, written and directed by Saju Ahmed. Kathak Nritya Shamproday, on Wednesday, staged a dance drama titled Shree Radhar Manvanjan, directed by Saju Ahmed. The festival also handed over Zinat Jahan Smriti Sammanana to Nilufar Wahid Papri on the opening day. Bulbul Academy of Fine Arts secretary Md Fazlur Rahaman was present as chief guest at the closing ceremony. Kathak Nritya Shamproday has been organising the festival since 2012.

title: Last-minute negotiations intensify
body: Today is the final day for submitting nomination papers for the upcoming 13th Jatiya Sangsad elections, triggering an intense last-minute political manoeuvring as parties race to finalise alliances and confirm their contesting line-ups. Smaller political parties remained engaged in the eleventh-hour negotiations with major political forces, seeking to secure electoral coalition or favourable seat-sharing arrangements before the window for nominations closes. Although there had been speculation that the deadline for submitting nomination papers might be extended, major parties, including the Bangladesh Nationalist Party and the Bangladesh Jamaat-e-Islami, have already finalised their respective strategic alliances and are set to submit nomination papers within the stipulated timeframe. The BNP has so far shared 16 seats with its movement partners. Meanwhile, the Jamaat on Sunday announced the expansion of its alliance to 10 parties from eight, following the inclusion of the National Citizen Party and the Liberal Democratic Party in the alliance. Sources said that the Jamaat-led alliance remained in the final stage of negotiations over seat-sharing arrangements. However, as of Sunday, the alliance had not disclosed how many seats would be allocated to each partner. Prior to joining the Jamaat-led bloc, both the NCP and the LDP had held talks with the BNP. However, they ultimately opted to get into the alliance with the Jamaat after failing to secure what they described as a sufficient number of seats from the BNP. Meanwhile, the Jatiya Party has begun preparations to submit nomination papers in almost all constituencies nationwide. The party is also holding discussions with leaders from other political groups, including those who have expressed dissatisfaction after being denied nominations by their own parties, notably the BNP. With the nomination deadline about to end, the country’s political landscape remains fluid as alliances are trying to solidify their positions and their contesting line-ups would take final shape ahead of the February polls. According to sources, although the BNP allocated 16 seats to its alliance partners, five of the candidates have already joined the party and will contest the election using the BNP’s electoral symbol, the sheaf of paddy. Candidates from BNP allies -- Islami Oikya Jote and the National People’s Party -- will also contest using the sheaf of paddy as their parties are not registered with the Election Commission. LDP secretary general Redwan Ahmed has joined the BNP and has been announced as the party’s candidate for Cumilla-7. Gono Odhikar Parishad general secretary Mohammad Rashed Khan has also joined the BNP and has been nominated as the party’s candidate for Jhenaidah-4. Bangladesh Jatiya Dal chair Syed Ahasanul Huda has dissolved his party and has joined the BNP. He will contest the parliamentary election from Kishoreganj-5 using the sheaf of paddy symbol. Bangladesh Liberal Democratic Party chair Shahadat Hossain Selim also dissolved his party and joined the BNP, after which he was named as the BNP candidate for Lakshmipur-1. In addition, Nationalist Democratic Movement chair Bobby Hajjaj has joined the BNP and will contest for Dhaka-13 using the party’s symbol. Meanwhile, Revolutionary Workers Party general secretary Saiful Haque will contest for Dhaka-12 using his party’s own symbol. Nagorik Oikya president Mahmudur Rahman Manna will contest for Bogra-2, Gono Odhikar Parishad president Nurul Haque Nur for Patuakhali-3, and Ganosamhati Andolan chief coordinator Zonayed Saki for Brahmanbaria-6, all under their respective party banners. BNP ally Bangladesh Jatiya Party chair Andaleeve Rahman Partho has submitted his nomination papers for the Bhola-1 constituency and announced that he would contest using his party’s cow cart symbol. The four candidates of Jamiat Ulema-e-Islam Bangladesh will contest the election with their own electoral symbol under the BNP-led alliance. Meanwhile, candidates for the upcoming election have collected a total of 2,780 nomination papers across the country, while only 31 have been submitted so far, according to an update from the Election Commission’s Central Coordination Committee as of 4:00pm on Sunday. Nomination papers can be collected and submitted daily from 9:00am to 5:00pm, with the submission window closing on Monday. Regional figures showed that the highest number of nomination papers collected in the Dhaka division was 501, followed by Comilla 405, Mymensingh 339, Khulna 302, Rangpur 283, Rajshahi 269, Chattogram 240, Barishal 161, Faridpur 145, and Sylhet 127. However, Faridpur leads with eight submissions, Mymensingh and Barishal seven each, Rangpur three, Dhaka and Chattogram two each, Khulna and Sylhet one each, while no nomination papers have been submitted from Rajshahi and Comilla so far. According to the election schedule, scrutiny would be carried out between December 30 and January 4, while January 20 has been set as the final date for withdrawal of candidature. The final list of candidates, along with election symbols, would be released on January 21. According to the schedule, appeals against returning officers’ decisions must be filed by January 9, with disposal scheduled between January 10 and 18. Election campaigning would run from January 22 until 7:30am on February 10, ending 48 hours before voting begins. Polling across all 300 parliamentary constituencies, as well as the national referendum, would take place on February 12 from 7:30am to 4:30pm.

title: Annual Urs of Khawaja Mainuddin Chisty (RA) held at Mia Saheb's Maidan
body: The annual Urs marking the 814th death anniversary of Hazrat Shah Sufi Khawaja Mainuddin Chisty Hasan Sanjeri Summa Azmeri (RA) was observed on Friday on the premises of Mia Saheb's Maidan at Luxmibazar in the Old Town of Dhaka. On the occasion, a discussion on the life and activities of Hazrat Khawaja Mainuddin Chisty (RA), along with a milad and doa mahfil, was organised after Maghrib prayers. Ninth Gaddinashin Peer Hazrat Maulana Shah Sufi Syed Ahamadur Rahim (Damat Barakatuhum), also the Mutwalli of Hazrat Shah Sufi Syed Abu Yousuf Abdullah (RA) Waqf Estate and director of Mia Saheb's Maidan Shah Saheb Bari Jamey Masjid, conducted the discussion. At the end of the programme, a doa mahfil and akheri munajat was held. The programme began with the recitation of verses from the Holy Quran by Dr Mohammed Ishtiaq Sazzadur Rahman, Hafez Md Faruq, and Hafez Mohammad Rahmatullah. Pesh Imam Mufti Qari Abdur Rahman Belali, a teacher at Qaderia Taheria Alim Madrasah, Trimohoni, Khilgaon, Dhaka, also the Khatib of Shah Saheb's Bari Jame Masjid, along with other Islamic scholars, delivered their religious speeches. The milad mahfil was conducted by Haji Sayed Barkatullah Badaruddin. Later, tabarruk was distributed among the devotees by convener of the programme Saiyed Taiyab Morshed Araf, said a press release.

title: SICIP participants in Jashore get loans from MTB
body: Mutual Trust Bank PLC has recently distributed loan sanction letters to selected participants of the Skills for Industry Competitiveness and Innovation Programme at the concluding ceremony of a month-long capacity-building workshop held in Jashore. Bangladesh Bank’s SME and Special Programmes Department director Nawshad Mustafa handed over the loan sanction letters as chief guest, said a press release. The SICIP programme is funded by the Asian Development Bank and implemented as an initiative of the Ministry of Finance. MTB Jashore branch organised the month-long workshop for 25 CMSME entrepreneurs, focusing on enhancing business management skills, product knowledge and financial literacy to support sustainable business growth. Addressing the ceremony, Nawshad Mustafa appreciated MTB’s initiative of sanctioning fresh loans to selected participants on the concluding day of the workshop. He noted that this timely financing reflected MTB’s strong commitment to strengthening CMSME financing activities and promoting inclusive economic growth across the country. Among others, SICIP project director and BB additional director Md Nazrul Islam, BB joint director Md Ayub Ali and MTB SME and agri banking division head Sanjib Kumar Dey were present at the event.

title: RFL Chair launches public awareness campaign
body: RFL Chair, houseware brand of business conglomerate RFL Group, has launched a public awareness campaign titled ‘Khomotar Noy, Somotar Chair,’ said a press release. RFL Group managing director RN Paul inaugurated the campaign at RFL Group’s head office in the capital’s Badda recently. Addressing the occasion, RN Paul said, ‘In Bangladesh’s political and social culture, the chair has long been regarded as a symbol of power. At public events, large, throne-like wooden chairs are reserved for senior leaders, high-ranking officials and influential individuals, while ordinary people are allocated plastic chairs or benches. Through this campaign, RFL wants to convey that a chair is a place to sit, not a measure of power.’ ‘Just as an ordinary voter can sit on an RFL chair, so can a public representative. There is no distinction between young and old, leaders and citizens. This message of equality is what RFL Chair wants to spread in society,’ he said. Toukirul Islam, deputy managing director of Durable Plastic Limited, said, ‘RFL is not taking any political stand through this campaign. We are just questioning a social practice. The objective of this campaign is to reduce the invisible distance that has been developed between public representatives and the ordinary people, at least in terms of thought.’ ‘We believe that power is not reflected in the design of a chair, but rather in people’s behaviour, values and sense of responsibility. RFL chair is highlighting that idea of equality,’ he added. Among others, RFL Houseware marketing head Esfaquel Hoque and brand manager Tonmoy Dev were present at the event.

title: NBR extends tax return submission to Jan 31
body: The government has extended the deadline for submitting income tax returns for individual taxpayers and Hindu undivided family taxpayers by another month for the 2025-26 tax year. According to an order issued by the National Board of Revenue, the return submission deadline has been extended from December 31, 2025, to January 31, 2026. The decision was taken in the public interest under the power conferred by Section 334 of the Income Tax Act, 2023, with prior approval from the government, the order added. The NBR had already extended the original deadline once, from November 30 to December 31, citing various practical difficulties faced by taxpayers. The latest extension aimed to provide additional time to facilitate wider compliance and ease pressure on taxpayers. The NBR has urged eligible taxpayers to avail themselves of the extended time and submit their returns within the revised deadline to avoid any inconvenience. Meanwhile, on December 21, NBR chairman Abdur Rahman Khan hinted that the deadline for online submission of income tax returns could be extended further, as a significant number of registered taxpayers have yet to file their returns digitally. In an event in the capital, he also said that NBR would assess progress based on submission trends. Around 4.2 million taxpayers have registered for online return submission, while more than 2.6 million have already filed their returns, he added, saying that around 1.5 to 1.6 million returns are still pending. ‘Receiving all of them within the next week might be difficult, especially as new registrations continue every day. On average, more than 15,000 taxpayers register daily for e-return submission,’ he added.

body: Kitchen markets see abundant supply of vegetables The prices of vegetables on wholesale and retail markets in the capital declined compared to that in recent weeks due to abundant supply, easing pressure on ordinary consumers. As school and work wrap up, crowds fill Tokyo’s many bustling arcade halls — not to battle it out in fighting games, but to snag plush toys from claw machines. BRAC Bank’s ATMs at the capital’s Pallabi, Mirpur-10, Farmgate, Shahbagh, and Bangladesh Secretariat stations of MRT Line-6 are now operational, said a press release. Bangladesh Foreign Exchange Dealers\' Association on Wednesday held its 32nd annual general meeting, said a press release. Cash transactions still dominated Bangladesh’s financial system in October 2025, accounting for 65.41 per cent of total transaction value, despite years of policy emphasis on building a cashless and digitally driven economy... Depositors of five crisis-hit Shariah-based banks that are being merged would be allowed to withdraw up to Tk 2 lakh each from Monday... Credit card use in Bangladesh recorded a sharp rise in October, with both domestic transactions and spending by Bangladeshis overseas increasing significantly compared to the previous month, according to the Bangladesh Bank... A month-long textile and cottage industries fair began in Rajshahi on Thursday, aiming to boost regional economy through revival and promotion of handloom and cottage products... The US oil company Chevron is walking a tightrope amid tensions between Washington and Caracas to retain its fragile position as the only foreign company allowed to exploit Venezuela’s oil reserves —- the largest in the world... Precious and industrial metals are surging to record highs as the year ends, driven by economic and geopolitical uncertainty, robust industrial demand and, in some cases, tight supply... Sales of cars made by Tesla, the company run by Elon Musk, have slumped nearly 40 per cent in the European Union this year, data from the European Automobile Manufacturers’ Association showed on Tuesday...

title: Business-Economy
body: Bangladesh interim govt to procure rice, edible oil, lentil to stabilise prices Bangladesh interim government has taken fresh initiatives to strengthen food security by approving proposals to procure 100,000 metric tons of rice, 4.75 crore liters of edible oil and 10,000 metric tons of lentil to meet the local growing demand aiming to stabilise prices and ensure smooth supply apparently ahead of the holy month of Ramadan.
