title: Candidates must declare income of dependents
body: The Election Commission has issued clarifications on nomination form requirements for the upcoming 13th Jatiya Sangsad elections, specifying that the candidates must disclose the income and assets of the fully dependent individuals. The commission has also clarified that providing income tax details for the spouses, children, and other dependents of the candidates is optional. The EC on Sunday issued the clarification hours after the Bangladesh Nationalist Party demanded clarification on the nomination form provision requiring candidates to disclose the income details of their children. BNP standing committee member Nazrul Islam Khan on Sunday met chief election commissioner AMM Nasir Uddin at the EC headquarters in Dhaka, seeking clarification on the nomination form provision that requires candidates to disclose their children’s income, despite the law mandating such disclosure only for dependents. Following the meeting, Nazrul Islam told reporters that the party raised concerns over the ‘confusing’ nomination form provision requiring candidates to disclose the income details of their children. He said that such a requirement could create complications because many children were financially independent, paid taxes separately, or live abroad, and that the Representation of the People Order mandates the disclosure only for the dependents. According to Nazrul Islam Khan, the CEC clarified that the form’s intention was to apply the provision only to dependent children, agreeing to issue a public notice to remove any ambiguity. The clarification would, the BNP leader said, benefit all candidates, including independents and those from other political parties. During the meeting, the BNP leader also stressed the growing risk posed by the misuse of technology and artificial intelligence on social media platforms, particularly for spreading propaganda and defamatory content. The party urged the EC to take strong measures, including identifying fake contents and taking legal action against the offenders, rather than relying solely on advisory measures. Replying to a question, Nazrul Islam said that seat-sharing arrangements with allied parties had been adjusted in 11 to 12 constituencies, though these were yet to be finalised. Answering a separate query, he confirmed that BNP acting chair Tarique would contest the upcoming election from Bogura, while any decision on his candidacy in Dhaka-17 would be formally announced by the party in due course.

title: Sealed with a kiss: Guardiola revels in Cherki starring role
body: Pep Guardiola is so smitten by Rayan Cherki that the Manchester City boss said he wanted to kiss the ‘incredible’ French star after his virtuoso performance in Saturday’s 2-1 win at Nottingham Forest. Cherki is fast emerging as City’s most influential playmaker in his first season in Manchester following a summer move from Lyon. The supremely gifted 22-year-old has sometimes left Guardiola frustrated after over-elaborating when a simple pass would be the better option, but he showcased his dazzling skill to great effect at the City Ground. Cherki set up Tijjani Reijnders’ second half opener with a perfectly weighted pass and then drilled City’s clinical late winner from just inside the area after Omari Hutchinson had levelled for Forest. ‘I want to allow him to express his incredible talent. We have to play better from the back so he can get more balls from that position. The second half was a little bit better,’ Guardiola said. ‘There are moments I shout at him and there are moments I want to kiss him.’ City’s sixth successive win in the Premier League sparked a jubilant response from Guardiola, who was serenaded by City’s travelling fans as he celebrated in front of them after the final whistle. Guardiola’s side were far from their best against gritty Forest, making the battling nature of their victory meaningful for the Spaniard. They often flopped in similar situations last season, including a 1-0 loss at the City Ground in March. And Guardiola admitted his side would have crumbled under the weight of Forest’s aggressive game-plan last term. Instead, they are firmly in the hunt for a title that would rank among Guardiola’s finest after his rebuilding work over the last 12 months. ‘I know the memory is weak but when we won the six Premier Leagues, these types of games have a lot, so this is a massive three points,’ he said. ‘Mainly for the quality of the opposition. Sean Dyche has created a proper team. It’s a top, top side. ‘It’s much more important how you suffer and defend and accept you are not playing good and accept you can be better. Otherwise there is no chance. Last season that game is lost 10 for 10.’

title: Future of RMG labour
body: IN BANGLADESH, the collapse of Rana Plaza in 2013 is remembered as a black day, and the tragedy continues to haunt those who survived it. Before engaging with the study of human rights, I too viewed the collapse largely as an accident, a catastrophic failure of a building that should never have housed factories. Over time, however, my understanding changed. Studying business and human rights made it impossible to see Rana Plaza as a mere accident. It was, instead, a brutal manifestation of a global supply chain model in which profit was prioritised over human life, and where poor workers, most of them women, were treated not as people, but as expendable inputs. For Asian countries leading the Ready-Made Garment industry, particularly Bangladesh, Rana Plaza stands as an enduring example of systemic failure in the governance of business and human rights. Twelve years after the collapse, the Ready-Made Garment sector has expanded significantly. Important improvements in factory building safety have been achieved, largely through legally binding initiatives such as the Accord on Fire and Building Safety and the Alliance for Bangladesh Worker Safety. Yet despite these developments, the sector now faces a more entrenched crisis: a widening gap between international legal commitments and the harsh commercial realities imposed by global buyers. The recent approval of three key International Labour Organisation conventions by Bangladesh’s interim government has opened a critical window for reform. However, whether these commitments translate into real change depends on how deeply global retailers embed these standards into their purchasing practices. Unequal pricing policies and the continued tolerance of opaque subcontracting arrangements are repeatedly cited as contributing factors behind labour violations and industrial disasters in the sector. Rana Plaza also exposed long-standing weaknesses within the domestic regulatory environment. Although labour laws existed long before 2013, enforcement mechanisms were persistently weak and in many respects remain so today. The Department of Inspection for Factories and Establishments has long been constrained by limited resources, institutional capacity and credibility, allowing violations to continue largely unchecked. More fundamentally, workers’ ability to act as their own monitors has been systematically undermined. Freedom of association, as guaranteed under International Labour Organisation convention no 87, and the Right to Organise and Collective Bargaining under convention no 98, have been eroded through bureaucratic barriers and widespread anti-union discrimination. Registering trade unions remains an arduous process and independent worker voices inside factories are frequently suppressed, weakening enforcement from the factory floor upward. Another persistent failure lies in the lack of sustained political attention from successive ruling governments. While rhetorical support for labour reform is often expressed, meaningful legislative progress has been slow. Amendments to labour laws are regularly delayed and frequently fall short of full compliance with International Labour Organisation standards. This failure is not merely administrative but deeply political. The economic dominance of the Ready-Made Garment sector has shielded factory owners from strict accountability, creating institutional tolerance for a low-wage, high-risk labour model that prioritises export competitiveness over worker safety and dignity. Yet the most decisive pressure within Bangladesh’s supply chain ecosystem is not generated in Dhaka or in Export Processing Zones. It originates in the sourcing offices of major Western brands. Global buying practices driven by fast fashion and relentless price competition have left Bangladeshi suppliers with little bargaining power. Low unit prices, tight lead times and delayed payments compress margins to the point where factories are forced to choose between financial survival and ethical compliance. Investments in occupational safety and health systems, payment of lawful overtime, or even maintaining minimum wages become increasingly difficult under these conditions. Evidence shows that the average unit price paid by European buyers has stagnated or declined, even as demands for sustainability and compliance continue to rise. This reality exposes the limitations of traditional Corporate Social Responsibility models. Voluntary commitments have repeatedly failed to prevent tragedies such as Rana Plaza and the Tazreen Fashion fire. In this context, mandatory Corporate Due Diligence frameworks offer a more credible path forward. The European Union’s Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive represents a significant regulatory shift. It requires large European Union and non-European Union companies operating within the European market to identify, prevent, mitigate and account for human rights and environmental harms across their operations and value chains. The directive rests on three core obligations. First, it extends accountability by allowing civil liability in European courts for failures in due diligence, creating legal avenues for compensation that did not exist after Rana Plaza. Second, it mandates value chain remediation by requiring brands to assess how their own purchasing practices including pricing, production timelines and payment terms contribute to harm within supplier factories. Third, it requires meaningful engagement with affected stakeholders, ensuring that workers, trade unions and labour-focused civil society organisations are formally involved in the design and implementation of due diligence measures. For Bangladesh, the importance of the Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive lies in its potential to close long-standing loopholes. Brands sourcing garments from Bangladesh would no longer be able to distance themselves from subcontracting practices or externalise human rights costs. They would be legally compelled to disclose complete supply chains, integrate human rights considerations into pricing decisions and ensure that orders do not foster labour exploitation or environmental harm. In this sense, the directive offers a shift from symbolic assurances to enforceable obligations. Domestically, the ratification of three International Labour Organisation conventions is a significant step forward. However, their practical value depends on implementation. The forthcoming Bangladesh Labour (Amendment) Ordinance, 2025, must be made genuinely accessible to the millions of workers it seeks to protect. At present, many conventions and policy documents remain available only in English, limiting their relevance for workers who cannot read foreign languages. Translating these materials into Bangla and disseminating them through worker organisations, non-governmental organisations and public education initiatives is essential. Without this effort, newly recognised rights will remain confined to technical documents rather than empowering those they are meant to serve. International researchers and academics continue to cite Rana Plaza as a defining symbol of Bangladesh’s garment industry, often to the country’s detriment. Yet the collapse also created an opportunity to reshape the sector’s narrative and move towards more ethical sourcing models, similar to those emerging in countries such as Sri Lanka. That opportunity has been repeatedly constrained by weak enforcement and short-term commercial priorities. Binding due diligence regulations such as the European Union’s Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive now present a renewed chance for systemic reform. Bangladesh has signed international agreements and taken formal steps towards reform. The remaining challenge lies with global brands. Resetting a supply chain long shaped by exploitation requires internalising the cost of human dignity, eliminating tolerance for unmonitored subcontracting and engaging meaningfully with organised workers. The commitments are in place. It is now for the world’s largest buyers to bear the responsibility of making them real. Shahenoor Akther Urmi, a freelance journalist, studies human rights and democratisation at Mahidol University, Thailand

title: Symptoms of sick society, failed governance
body: THE killing of Dipu Chandra Das at Bhaluka in Mymensingh on December 18, followed by the public burning of his body, once again marks a moral nadir that should shame a nation. The young man, an employee of a local apparel factory, was beaten to death by what appears to be an organised mob. After killing the young man, the mob dragged his body to the Dhaka–Mymensingh Highway and set fire to it. The alleged provocation was that he had hurt religious sentiments. Yet, no one has so far been able to produce anything — a single sentence, posting or utterance — that explains what he supposedly said. He did not even have any social media account. While the presence of such remarks, if there is any, would not justify what happened to him, the absence matters. It suggests that it was not merely a crime of rage but a crime of convenience. A man was targeted, dehumanised and erased for reasons that remain unstated while religion served as the ready alibi. Such acts are often explained through the language of fury and religious sentiment: people ‘lost control’ or emotions ‘boiled over.’ Rage theory, however, offers a more disturbing and more accurate lens. Rage, as psychologists note, is not a spontaneous explosion. It is a social process. It grows when grievances are rehearsed and manipulated, identities hardened and ring-fenced, and enemies named. It thrives in crowds where it is easy to diffuse responsibility and turn cruelty into performance. At Bhaluka, the beating was not a momentary loss of temper. It was organised. The burning of the body was not an accident. It was a message. Rage here was not blind. It was directed, ritualised and applauded. What makes this episode chilling is the crowd’s conduct after death. There was no withdrawal or hesitation and no collective realisation that a line had been crossed. Instead, there was inaction — and worse, a vicious joy — when the body was burnt on a highway. This is rage turned into spectacle that tells us more about the state of society and the failure of governance than any shouted slogans. When death elicits celebration rather than horror, the moral brakes have failed. Alarming as it is, the incident is not an isolated incident, an aberration. It is part of a grim pattern that reflects the cumulative deterioration of law and order and the failure of the state to stop them and impose consequences. Allegations of hurting religious sentiments have repeatedly been used to unleash violence against individuals and groups. The threshold for offence has dropped so low that it no longer needs content; accusation alone suffices. That is why the inability to identify what the young man actually said is not a minor detail but a significant core of the story. When evidence is unnecessary, guilt becomes a social verdict delivered by the loudest crowd. The wider context makes the danger unmistakable. Organised mobs have attacked Sufi practitioners and shrines at an alarming frequency in recent times. On September 5, a mob even exhumed the body of a Sufi practitioner and burned it in daylight. This is an act so grotesque that it defies comprehension. Since August 8, 2024, when the interim government assumed office after the fall of the authoritarian Awami League regime, more than a hundred shrines, cultural and religious sites have reportedly been attacked which left dozens of devotees injured. Petty thieves and alleged offenders have been beaten to death by mobs frequently. Each of such incidents chips away at the rule of law and together they normalise it. Violence multiplies when it goes unpunished. Rage feeds on impunity. When perpetrators of earlier attacks are not brought to justice, violence becomes a rational choice within a perverse moral economy. The crowd learns that brutality carries little cost and may even earn social approval. People learn that silence is safer than intervention. Law enforcement learns that delay is acceptable. Over time, rage becomes embedded in expectations and become a routine. This is where the failure of the authorities becomes pivotal. In case after case, the law enforcement agencies have been slow to act, inadequately prepared or conspicuously absent. Statements of condemnation arrive after incidents, polished and hollow. Investigations stall; arrests, if any, are selective. The message received by the street is unmistakable. You may act first; the state will respond later, if at all. At Bhaluka, the mob did not fear interruption while beating a man to death nor while burning the body on the highway. That confidence did not emerge overnight. Responsibility does not end with the police. The government has treated mob violence as an optic problem rather than a governance failure. Condemnations substitute for consequences. Commissions substitute for convictions. Meanwhile, those who claim moral authority — religious scholars, community leaders and civil society — have, too, often been timid or indifferent. When mobs vandalise shrines or lynch individuals in the name of faith, equivocation is complicity. Silence is not neutrality. It is permission. The targeting of minorities adds another layer of urgency. The victim at Bhaluka was a Hindu young man in a predominantly Muslim country. That fact cannot be scrubbed out. When a minority individual is accused of hurting sentiments and the crowd acts with such ferocity, the imbalance of power is obvious. Rage is easier to unleash against those already marked as vulnerable. The absence of evidence about the alleged offence strengthens the suspicion that the accusation masked other motives — local disputes, labour tension and personal vendettas — laundered through religious outrage to mobilise numbers and immunity. A society that permits or tolerates this corrodes its own future. Mob culture is incompatible with democratic ideals. It replaces due process with instant justice and truth with noise. It teaches the young that cruelty is courage and that belonging requires participation in violence or acquiescence to it. Once learnt, the lessons do not stay confined to religious disputes. They spill over to politics, workplaces and neighbourhoods. What, then, must be done? First, the government must acknowledge failure without euphemism. Law and order is not an abstract aspiration. It is a daily practice. Perpetrators of the killing must be brought to justice. Second, earlier incidents, including attacks on Sufi shrines and mob killings, must be reopened where justice has been denied. Impunity must be reversed, not managed. Third, policing must be proactive. Intelligence, rapid response and clear rules of engagement are essential when rumours of offence circulate. Waiting for violence to erupt before acting is not restraint; it is abdication. Fourth, political leaders and religious scholars must speak plainly and consistently: no allegations of offence justify violence; no crowd stands above the law. Finally, society must confront the mirror. The most damning image from Bhaluka is not only the killing but the crowd’s reaction to the burning body — the inaction, smiles and the sense of occasion. That is the symptom of a deep sickness. A society heals only when it relearns to see the other as human, to respect the faith of others. Until then, rage will continue to masquerade as faith, accusation as proof and spectacle as justice. And more bodies will burn on the roads while we tell ourselves that it was inevitable. It is not. It is chosen, by mobs, by silence and by a state that has yet to decide whether it will rule by law or be ruled by the crowd. Monwarul Islam is an assistant editor at New Age.

title: Myanmar junta stages election after five years of civil war
body: Voters trickled to Myanmar’s heavily restricted polls on Sunday, with the ruling junta touting the exercise as a return to democracy five years after it ousted the last elected government and triggered a civil war. Former civilian leader Aung San Suu Kyi remains jailed, while her hugely popular party has been dissolved and was not taking part. Campaigners, Western diplomats and the United Nations’ rights chief have all condemned the phased month-long vote, citing a ballot stacked with military allies and a stark crackdown on dissent. The pro-military Union Solidarity and Development Party is widely expected to emerge as the largest bloc, in what critics say would be a rebranding of martial rule. ‘We guarantee it to be a free and fair election,’ junta chief Min Aung Hlaing told reporters after casting his ballot in the capital Naypyidaw. ‘It’s organised by the military, we can’t let our name be tarnished.’ The Southeast Asian nation of around 50 million people is riven by civil war and there will be no voting in areas controlled by rebel factions that have risen up to challenge military rule. While opposition factions threatened to attack the election, there were no reports of violence against polling day activities by the time voting ended at 4:00pm (0930 GMT). Snaking queues of voters formed for the previous election in 2020, which the military declared void a few months later when it ousted Aung San Suu Kyi and seized power. But when a polling station near her vacant home closed on Sunday, only around 470 of its roughly 1,700 registered voters had cast ballots, an election official said — a turnout of less than 28 per cent. Its first voter, Bo Saw, 63, said the election ‘will bring the best for the country’. ‘The first priority should be restoring a safe and peaceful situation,’ he said. At a downtown Yangon station near the gleaming Sule Pagoda — the site of huge pro-democracy protests after the 2021 coup — 45-year-old Swe Maw dismissed international criticism. ‘There are always people who like and dislike,’ he said at a polling station that later reported a turnout of below 37 per cent. The run-up saw none of the feverish public rallies that Aung San Suu Kyi once commanded, and the junta has waged a withering pre-vote offensive to claw back territory. ‘I don’t think this election will change or improve the political situation in this country,’ said 23-year-old Hman Thit, displaced by the post-coup conflict. ‘I think the air strikes and atrocities on our hometowns will continue,’ he said in a rebel-held area of Pekon township in Shan state. The military ruled Myanmar for most of its post-independence history, before a 10-year interlude saw a civilian government take the reins in a burst of optimism and reform. However, Min Aung Hlaing snatched power in a coup, alleging widespread voter fraud, after Aung San Suu Kyi’s National League for Democracy party trounced pro-military opponents in the 2020 elections. The military put down pro-democracy protests and many activists quit the cities to fight as guerrillas alongside ethnic minority armies that have long held sway in Myanmar’s fringes. There is no official death toll for Myanmar’s civil war and estimates vary widely, but global conflict monitoring group ACLED tallies media reports of violence and estimates that 90,000 people have been killed on all sides since the coup. Aung San Suu Kyi is serving a 27-year sentence on charges that rights groups dismiss as politically motivated. ‘I don’t think she would consider these elections to be meaningful in any way,’ her son Kim Aris said from his home in Britain. Most parties from the 2020 vote, including Aung San Suu Kyi’s, have since been dissolved. The Asian Network for Free Elections says 90 per cent of the seats in the previous election went to organisations that did not appear on Sunday’s ballots. New electronic voting machines did not allow write-in candidates or spoiled ballots. The junta is pursuing prosecutions against more than 200 people for violating draconian legislation forbidding ‘disruption’ of the poll, including protest or criticism. The United Nations in Myanmar said it was ‘critical that the future of Myanmar is determined through a free, fair, inclusive and credible process that reflects the will of its people’. The second round of polling will take place in two weeks before the third and final round on January 25, but the junta has acknowledged that elections cannot happen in almost one in five lower house constituencies.

title: Teknaf, Ukhia border shaken in Myanmar explosion
body: The bordering areas along Teknaf and Ukhia upazilas in Cox’s Bazar and Naikhyangchari upazila in Bandarban were shaken in powerful explosions near the areas inside civil war-ridden Myanmar on Saturday night. Panic gripped the areas as the explosions could be heard from the Whykong union of Teknaf upazila, Palangkhali and Rajapalang unions of Ukhia upazila and Ghumdhum union of Naikhyangchari upazila, said the locals and the members of the union councils. In Whykong union, villagers said, the intensity of the explosions was felt at about 10:45pm on Saturday and the houses in the area trembled due to the explosions. Abul Hasnat, a resident of the Unchiprang area of Whykong, said that a series of loud explosions suddenly shook the entire locality. Children and elderly people inside houses began screaming in fear, he added. Another resident, Maulana Jasim Uddin, said that the explosions were so strong that he initially thought that it was an earthquake. Out of panic, he rushed outside with his family members to take shelter, he said. He said that some of the inhabitants in his locality left home at night in fear but returned to their homes in the morning as no explosion could be heard later at night. Teknaf upazila nirbahi officer Md Emamul Hafiz Nadim said that they, after receiving the information, contacted the Border Guard Bangladesh. ‘Residents of the border areas were also alerted and necessary measures were taken to ensure their safety,’ he said. According to sources, clashes between Myanmar’s junta forces and the armed group Arakan Army are continuing in Rakhine State. Sounds of gunfire could be heard earlier from Teknaf bordering areas on the nights following December 13 and December 17 due to intense fighting inside Myanmar.

title: Development without safeguards
body: THE ecosystem is a complex entity that functions in a coordinated manner, maintaining a delicate balance among its constituents. The present global ecosystem is the cumulative outcome of adaptations and adjustments to natural shocks over millions of years. Natural ecosystems therefore possess an inherent capacity to absorb external shocks — but this capacity is not unlimited. Ecosystems began functioning around 350 million years ago (Topsoil and Civilization, 1955), long before humanity came into being, after most ecosystem services were already in operation. Initially, humankind was a child of nature; ecosystem dysfunction began soon after humans assumed the role of master of nature. To meet the growing and increasingly diverse demands of the global population, humans have exerted enormous pressure on ecosystems through, for example, agricultural and industrial revolutions, without due regard to the limits of tolerance to developmental shocks. As a result of technological hazards, anthropogenic shocks—now surpassing natural ones—have exceeded the buffering and carrying capacity of global ecosystems, leading to resource depletion and global warming. Global warming represents a profound failure of the principle of ‘grow first, clean later’. Industrialisation has caused severe degradation of soil, water and air. Many water bodies around the world — such as the Thames in London, the Rhine in Germany, Dokai Bay in Japan and the Han River in Korea—became ecologically dysfunctional, or effectively ‘dead’, due to severe pollution, although they are said to have been restored later. Economic development was achieved at the cost of intense pollution. But what of other components of the global ecosystem, such as soil and the atmosphere? Soil contamination by persistent organic pollutants (POPs) and the accumulation of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere, driving global warming, continue to haunt people across continents. Bangladesh is no exception to this development path. To feed a growing population from limited natural resources, Bangladesh transformed its agriculture through the so-called Green Revolution, relying on high-yielding variety crops and heavy use of agrochemicals, causing large-scale land degradation. Industrialisation began in the 1980s, and its subsequent growth has led to massive environmental pollution, despite ample global evidence of development shocks and their deadly consequences. We failed to learn from the history of so-called development. We did not consider the shock-absorption capacity of our ecosystems; instead, we traded away our natural resources—soil fertility, water and air quality — beyond their tolerance limits. Greedy and unplanned development has turned many ecosystems into Ecologically Critical Areas (ECAs), meaning they no longer function properly and require intensive care. The ECAs declared by the Government of Bangladesh include the Sundarbans (10km around the reserve forest), Cox’s Bazar–Teknaf sea beach, St Martin’s Island, Sonadia Island, Hakaluki Haor, Tanguar Haor, Marzat Baor, Gulshan–Baridhara Lake, the Buriganga, Turag, Balu and Shitalakhya rivers and their foreshore areas, and the Jaflong–Dauki River. From independence to the present day, numerous development projects have been implemented by various agencies, and the ultimate outcome is that many of these areas are now ecologically critical — glaring examples of unplanned development. Data show that the Dhaleshwari and many other rivers are moving towards ECA status. Global and national politics of pollution — sometimes designed to appease polluters and often creating disparities in the business landscape — along with transboundary pollution and overexploitation of resources, have further impoverished our environment. At times, multinational companies shift their most polluting operations from highly regulated industrialised countries to nations seeking foreign investment, cheap labour and operating under lax environmental standards (Markham, 1994). The removal of garments and sweater production from the Orange-B category of the Environment Conservation Rules (ECR) 1997 in 2007, keeping it beyond environmental accounting despite its adverse impacts, is another example of such politics. Moreover, the lack of environmental education and awareness, weak anti-pollution forces, poor leadership, corruption, inadequate legal instruments and inconsistent enforcement have all contributed to massive environmental degradation. Unplanned industrialisation, failure in waste management by excluding treatment systems from project design, and persistent refusal to pay for pollution loads have subjected the nation’s ecosystems to shocks of an unprecedented scale. The consequences are visible in rising disease burdens, reduced productivity and mounting social costs. Economically developed nations attained per capita incomes exceeding $30,000 by polluting their rivers and other resources. In Bangladesh, our per capita income remains around $2,600, yet we already have thirteen ECAs and counting. The question then arises: how many more ECAs must we create to become economically developed? Are we even capable of providing intensive care for existing ECAs, or protecting other ecosystems from meeting the same fate? The emptiness of the ‘grow first, clean later’ idea has been exposed — it leaves a lasting environmental burden. Globally, there is ample scientific and technological support for pursuing growth while cleaning simultaneously. It is therefore essential to reorient our approach towards environmentally friendly investment and to rethink our development trajectory. More people mean greater demand for food, jobs and services, which in turn require development. Yet development, if poorly designed, inevitably shocks ecosystems. Depletion of natural resources, both in quantity and quality, undermines production processes and ultimately erodes development itself. To sustain development, we must mitigate development shocks, ensuring that residual impacts do not exceed the carrying capacity of the ecosystems we inhabit. We must also cut our coat according to the cloth of our natural resources. This requires optimising population size relative to resources, moderating consumption patterns and managing household goods sustainably. Clear commitments to pollution abatement by concerned sectors and agencies are essential. Equally crucial are appropriate legal instruments, their strict enforcement and capacity-building within relevant institutions. Broad public engagement in environmental conservation is vital. Training teachers and religious leaders could be an effective means of nurturing an eco-sensitive generation. Investment in children remains the best pathway to achieving the much-needed sustainable development that meets present needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet theirs. Dr Md Sohrab Ali is a former additional director general at the Department of Environment.

title: Dhaka Drama stages ‘Abibhakta’ in US
body: The United States-based Bangladeshi artistes of the theatre troupe Dhaka Drama has staged a production based on Liberation War titled Undivided in Bronx, New York in the US. Based on the story of the Liberation War in exile through interactive theatre, the second performance of the play was staged at an event titled Victory Festival organised by Hridoye Bangladesh. The play, directed by Golam Sarwar Harun and Gargi Mukherjee based on a docu-novel by Hasan Ferdous, highlights the role of expatriates living in New York in Bangladesh’s struggle for independence. It also reflects an attempt to investigate the root causes of the current political instability in Bangladesh. The script has been adapted by Golam Sarwar Harun. Laila Farzana, an artiste of the play, told New Age that the audience enjoyed the play with rapt attention. ‘As it was an interactive play, the distance between the performers and the audience was eliminated, and everyone seemed to become one,’ she added. Golam Sarwar Harun, Ejaz Alam, Pratima Sumi, Laila Farzana, Basunia Sumon, Ripon Rahman, Md Kajol, Monir Hossain and Sajjad Rahman Khan have portrayed different roles in the production. Notably, the first staging of Undivided took place on the occasion of World Theatre Day at the Jamaica Centre for Arts and Learning on March 27.

title: ‘Consonancy of Fantasy’ presents Ctg-based artists’ works in Dhaka
body: Five Chattogram-based contemporary artists displayed their artworks at a group art exhibition titled ‘Consonancy of Fantasy’, which is under way at Safiuddin Shilpalay of Dhanmondi in the capital. A five-day exhibition comprising drawings, paintings and scroll paintings created on paper and canvas, as well as four iron sculptures, was inaugurated on Friday. Artists Sanjoy Kumar Das, Uttam Kumer Talukder, Sanjib Barua, Jaber Ahmed Chowdhury, and Arun Kumar Shil portrayed contemporary issues and crises, specifically those of the post-pandemic era. Sanjoy Kumar Das’s acrylic on canvas, titled Life through Vaccination 3, depicts multiple layered events from the pandemic, focusing primarily on sick people and their tense activities at the hospital. Uttam Kumer Talukder’s canvas consisted of multi-layered events and symbols, Sanjib Barua’s shows the brutality of time, and Arun Kumar Shil’s drawing also juxtaposes diverse images. Jaber Ahmed Chowdhury’s two-dimensional iron sculptures depict the joy and sorrows of life with minimal blocks. The exhibition will end today.

title: Rowa-Daw portrays hill life of Bandarban
body: Bandarban-based young visual artist Khing Shai Mong Marma’s first solo painting exhibition, titled ‘Rowa-Daw’, which portrays the hill life of Bandarban, will end today at the Ethnic Cultural Institute in Bandarban. In the Marma vocabulary, ‘Rowa’ means a neighbourhood or village and ‘Daw’ is a word of respect, the term used to consider that village as a place of honour. A four-day exhibition featuring 27 paintings was inaugurated on December 19 and the collection which includes charcoal, oil on canvas, and watercolours, depicts the struggle of national minority people alongside the natural beauty of hills and rivers and colourful culture of the people. Coming from the Marma community, artist Khing Shai Mong has chosen the heritage of his ethnic group as the subject of paintings. Raised on hilly areas, he expresses the essence of the landscape, people and lifestyle of various animals that the hill people have understood for generations. An oil-on-canvas painting titled Stone shows several stones tied together, the stones protect the land, but people are stealing them, which has created an environmental threat. Oil on canvas titled Existence 3 shows twelve reptiles on the face of an old woman, the faded creatures symbolise the fading indigenous tribes of the hills. The watercolour on paper titled Shangu River 1 shows the landscape of the bank of the River Shangu while the water carries the reflection of the hilltop village. The exhibition displayed artworks in a makeshift gallery because Bandarban lacks a dedicated exhibition space and according to artist Khing Shai Mong, this is the first solo exhibition ever held in the city. Khing Shai Mong Marma graduated from the University of Development Alternative and participated in many group art exhibitions across the country.

title: 2-day Hason Raja folk festival begins today
body: The two-day Hason Raja Folk Festival 2025 will begin in Sylhet today, marking the birth anniversary of the poet. Organised by the Hason Raja Folk Literature and Culture Council, the festival will be held on the Central Shaheed Minar premises in Chowhatta area in Sylhet. Programmes will run daily from 3:30pm to 10:00pm. The festival will showcase various aspects of Hason Raja’s life, philosophy and folk heritage through discussions, cultural performances, recitations and renditions of his songs. Jahirul Islam Achinpuri, president of the central committee of the Hasan Raja Folk Literature and Culture Council, said, ‘The birth anniversary of Hasan Raja is on December 21.’ The council has been working to revive Bengal’s traditional Sufi culture with the aim of promoting a non-violent, intellectual, creator-centred and afterlife-centred society, he mentioned. Researchers, artistes, litterateurs and cultural activists from different parts of the country are expected to participate in the festival, he added, noting that enthusiasm had already been created in Sylhet’s cultural arena surrounding the event. Achinpuri also said that the festival was originally scheduled to begin on Saturday, December 20, but was deferred by a day in observance of the mourning day announced by the government for the demise of Sharif Osman Bin Hadi. The organisers urged people from all walks of life to attend the festival with their families.
